assignment_policy: Papers can appear under multiple themes. The mathematical and algorithmic foundations theme is the shared baseline for this sequence-alignment literature collection; all other assignments require substantive support in report features. Incidental mentions and references alone are excluded.

themes.label: Mathematical and algorithmic foundations

papers.title: Fast string matching with k differences
indicators: The authors state that their algorithms are asymptotically faster than O(mn) dynamic programming only when k² = o(m). (PDF p. 3).
The first preprocessing method stores longest common-prefix lengths for pairs of pattern suffixes in MAX-LENGTH. A diagonal recurrence fills this table in O(m²) time. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: A Time Efficient Algorithm for Finding Longest Common Subsequence from two Molecular Sequences
indicators: The authors propose a sequential LCS algorithm that stores database-sequence positions in nucleotide-specific buckets. (PDF p. 1).
The authors aim to reduce the time needed to find an LCS between a stored DNA sequence and a query sequence. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Protein remote homology detection and structural alignment using deep learning
indicators: Differentiable Needleman–Wunsch uses logsumexp and softmax to produce an expected traceback matrix. Directional derivatives and local Hessians support training. Cross-entropy compares predicted alignment probabilities with TM-align reference alignments. (PDF p. 13).

DeepBLAST was evaluated against manually curated Malidup and Malisam alignments. Table 2 compares alignment F1 scores with BLAST, HMMER, Needleman–Wunsch, Smith–Waterman and four structural alignment methods. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: SAUTE: sequence assembly using target enrichment
indicators: The authors develop SAUTE and SAUTE_PROT to assemble target nucleotide and protein sequences directly from short reads. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: WFA-GPU: gap-affine pairwise read-alignment using GPUs
indicators: The authors present WFA-GPU, a GPU-accelerated pairwise sequence aligner based on the wavefront alignment algorithm. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: TM-align: A Protein Structure Alignment Algorithm Based on the TM-score
indicators: The authors present TM-align, a protein structure alignment algorithm that optimizes TM-score rather than RMSD. (PDF p. 1).
TM-align combines dynamic programming with heuristic rotation matrices to align protein tertiary structures. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Rapid and Sensitive Protein Similarity Searches
indicators: High-scoring diagonal regions are identified and joined, followed by local dynamic programming optimization. (PDF p. 1).
Filtering matches by shared diagonal offsets avoids computing the full dynamic programming matrix. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Clifford Group Equivariant Neural Network Layers for Protein Structure Prediction
indicators: The authors replace linear layers in a protein-coordinate projector with Clifford Group Equivariant Neural Network layers. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A survey of sequence alignment algorithms for next-generation sequencing
indicators: Hash-based methods use seed and extend. BLAST indexes query k-mers, scans for exact matches, extends and joins seeds, and refines alignments with Smith–Waterman. (PDF p. 2).
SIMD vectorization processes several query positions per CPU cycle. The cited SSE2 Smith–Waterman implementation is reported to exceed a tenfold speedup over the standard algorithm. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: An Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence and Substring Problem for Multiple Strings
indicators: When all endpoint symbols match, the recurrence decrements every index and adds one to the previous length. (PDF p. 16).
When the common Y symbol differs from X endpoint symbols, the recurrence decrements the mismatching X indices and retains the Y indices. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: A trimodal protein language model enables advanced protein searches
indicators: ProTrek learns a shared representation of protein sequence, structure, and function text through bidirectional contrastive learning. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: New Processor Array Architectures for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors propose linear and block processor arrays for a bit-level dynamic programming algorithm for longest common subsequences. (PDF p. 1).
Interpretation: the eight-processor LCS estimate is about 40% above the measured time. This weakens the authors' description of close agreement for that case. (PDF p. 17).

papers.title: Algorithms for Jumbled Indexing, Jumbled Border and Jumbled Square on run-length encoded strings
indicators: The authors study jumbled indexing, borders, and squares on run-length encoded strings. Jumble matching requires equal symbol histograms. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Computing a Longest Common Subsequence for Multiple Sequences
indicators: The authors propose RepeDPH and MRepeDPH to find long common subsequences through repeated two-string dynamic programming. (PDF p. 2).
They aim to improve the string ordering used by repeated pairwise LCS computation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: The String-to-String Correction Problem
indicators: The authors formalize the string-to-string correction problem and present the classic O(mn) dynamic programming algorithm. (PDF p. 1).
Edit distance is defined as the minimum-cost sequence of character insertions, deletions, and substitutions. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A coarse-grained multicomputer parallel algorithm for the sequential substring constrained longest common subsequence problem
indicators: The authors parallelize the sequential substring constrained longest common subsequence problem on the CGM model. The result must contain the specified constraint strings in order. (PDF p. 1).
The authors propose future use of the method for LCS problems with multiple inclusion or exclusion constraints. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: Progressive Sequence Alignment as a Prerequisite to Correct Phylogenetic Trees
indicators: The algorithm calculates pairwise alignment scores using dynamic programming. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Longest common subsequence between run-length-encoded strings: a new algorithm with improved parallelism
indicators: RLE-LCS computes the longest common subsequence length from run-length-encoded strings. It updates block boundaries instead of all dynamic programming entries. (PDF p. 3).
The authors aim to reduce LCS computation while preserving parallelism through operations that use sums and comparisons. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Next-Generation Sequence Assembly: Four Stages of Data Processing and Computational Challenges
indicators: The authors organize next-generation sequence assembly into four stages: preprocessing filtering, graph construction, graph simplification, and postprocessing filtering. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Approximating the Longest Common Subsequence problem within a sub-polynomial factor in linear time
indicators: The author presents a randomized algorithm that estimates LCS within an n^{o(1)} factor in O(n) time, with high probability. (PDF p. 2).
The algorithm reduces LCS to Block-LIS and uses an existing Block-LIS approximation algorithm. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein-to-genome alignment with miniprot
indicators: Miniprot maps proteins to complete genomes with a seed-chain-extend algorithm and spliced dynamic programming. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and Flexible String Matching by Combining Bit-parallelism and Suffix Automata
indicators: The authors introduce Backward Nondeterministic Dawg Matching (BNDM). It combines suffix automata with bit-parallel simulation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast multiple alignment of ungapped DNA sequences using information theory and a relaxation method
indicators: Malign aligns ungapped nucleic-acid sequences by maximizing total sequence information in a selected window. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BIMSA: accelerating long sequence alignment using processing-in-memory
indicators: BIMSA implements BiWFA on the UPMEM processing-in-memory platform to reduce sequence-alignment data movement. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Special Case of the Maximal Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The abstract states an O(n log n) running time for the restricted common subsequence problem. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: On the Economical Construction of the Transitive Closure of a Directed Graph
indicators: The authors construct the transitive closure of an acyclic directed graph in O(n³/ln n) operations. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Survey on Sequence Alignment Algorithms and State-of-the-Art Aligners
indicators: The authors organize pairwise and multiple sequence aligners by common algorithmic stages. Their literature collection contains 158 documents. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Parallel Algorithm for Longest Common Subsequence in a String
indicators: The authors propose a parallel dynamic programming algorithm for LCS. The C implementation uses OpenMP. (PDF p. 3).
The authors aim to reduce computation time for LCS comparisons of two DNA strings or patterns. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast Algorithms for the Shortest Unique Palindromic Substring Problem on Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: The authors develop data structures for shortest unique palindromic substring queries on run-length encoded strings. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: pLM-BLAST: distant homology detection based on direct
indicators: Local scoring uses a modified Smith-Waterman procedure without gap penalties or zero truncation. Traceback starts from sequence boundaries to generate multiple candidate paths. (PDF p. 2).
Global mode uses Needleman-Wunsch with the embedding-based substitution matrix and a zero gap penalty. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Approximate Multiple Pattern String Matching using Bit Parallelism: A Review
indicators: The paper describes BNDM for single-pattern search and a Shift OR filter for multiple-pattern search. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BAli-Phy version 3: model-based co-estimation of alignment and phylogeny
indicators: BAli-Phy uses MCMC to jointly estimate alignment, phylogeny, and evolutionary parameters from unaligned sequences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast text searching: allowing errors
indicators: Wu and Manber extend a bit-array exact-matching method to approximate matching with insertions, deletions, and substitutions. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast, sensitive detection of protein homologs using deep dense retrieval
indicators: DHR retrieves protein homologs through learned sequence embeddings and dot-product similarity. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Accurate Prediction of Protein Structures and Interactions Using a Three-Track Neural Network
indicators: RoseTTAFold exchanges information between sequence alignments, residue-pair geometry, and three-dimensional coordinates in a three-track neural network. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Sketching, Streaming, and Fine-Grained Complexity of (Weighted) LCS
indicators: The authors prove lower bounds for LCS sketching and streaming, and settle the fine-grained complexity of weighted LCS. (PDF p. 1).
Under SETH, computing weighted LCS requires (nm)^(1-o(1)) time over constant-size alphabets. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Optimal Gap-Affine Alignment in O(s) Space
indicators: The gap-affine model assigns cost x to a mismatch and o + le to a gap of length l. WFA extends farthest-reaching offsets with longest common prefixes. (PDF p. 2).
BiWFA alternates forward and reverse wavefront computation. Reverse extension uses longest common suffixes. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Finding Approximate Patterns in Strings
indicators: The report is part of the sequence-alignment literature corpus.

papers.title: BetaAlign: a deep learning approach for multiple sequence alignment
indicators: BetaAlign trains transformers to convert unaligned sequences into multiple sequence alignments using simulated training examples. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: MMseqs2 supports protein sequence searches and iterative profile searches. It combines similar-k-mer filtering, vectorized ungapped alignment, and gapped Smith-Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 1).
Candidates pass through vectorized ungapped alignment and then gapped Smith-Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Survey on Longest Common Subsequence
indicators: The authors compare LCS methods and their use in sequence comparison. They distinguish length calculation from subsequence reconstruction. (PDF p. 1).
The proposed changes remove empty prefixes and the zero boundary row and column from the dynamic programming table. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: A New Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors propose an LCS algorithm that uses ordered match pairs for two DNA sequences. (PDF p. 1).
The authors aim to reduce the time and space needed to find an LCS. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Accelerating Cryptanalysis with the Method of Four Russians
indicators: Bard describes M4RI for dense Boolean linear systems. The paper gives a cost analysis and experimental runtime measurements. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Fast Algorithm for Computing Longest Common Subsequences
indicators: The authors present an LCS algorithm with O((r + n) log n) time, where r counts matching position pairs in two sequences of length n. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm recovers an actual LCS and uses O(r + n) space. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: CLUSTAL W: Improving the Sensitivity of Progressive Multiple Sequence Alignment Through Sequence Weighting, Position-Specific Gap Penalties and Weight Matrix Choice
indicators: Initial pairwise comparisons can use fast k-tuple alignment or full dynamic programming. Identity scores are converted to differences per site without correction for multiple substitutions. (PDF p. 3).
Each progressive step uses full dynamic programming to align two sequences or existing alignments. Gaps in existing alignments remain fixed. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: RecGraph: recombination-aware alignment of sequences to variation graphs
indicators: The authors formalize the recombination-aware alignment problem as an optimal path switch under dynamic programming. (PDF p. 5).
Dynamic programming alignments allow switching between graph paths subject to affine recombination penalties. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Protein Structure Comparison by Alignment of Distance Matrices
indicators: The authors introduce the DALI algorithm for comparing 3D protein structures using 2D distance matrices. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Strobealign: flexible seed size enables ultra-fast and accurate read alignment
indicators: The author introduces strobealign, a short-read aligner based on variable-size syncmer and randstrobe seeding. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Next Generation Sequence Analysis and Computational Genomics Using Graphical Pipeline Workflows
indicators: The Graphical Pipeline for Computational Genomics integrates workflows from raw DNA sequencing reads through variant calling and annotation. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A*PA2: Up to 19× Faster Exact Global Alignment
indicators: A*PA2 computes exact global pairwise alignments under edit distance. It combines band doubling, bitpacking, block computation, and A* heuristics. (PDF p. 1).
The goal is to combine A*PA's near-linear runtime on similar sequences with the efficiency of dynamic programming. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Edit Distance in Near-Linear Time: it’s a Constant Factor
indicators: The authors present a randomized constant-factor approximation for edit distance. For each fixed ε > 0, its running time is O(n^(1+ε)). (PDF p. 3).
The algorithm builds distance oracles across increasing substring lengths. These oracles approximate substring distances in an average sense sufficient to estimate the full edit distance. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Fast Bit-Vector Algorithm for Approximate String Matching Based on Dynamic Programming
indicators: A second algorithm uses the bit-vector computation within a dynamic programming zone. The stated expected time is O(kn/w) for unrestricted pattern length. (PDF p. 3).
Encoding differences between adjacent dynamic programming entries removes the dependence on k from the basic algorithm's time bound. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Bilingual language model for protein sequence and structure
indicators: Global Needleman–Wunsch alignment with the Foldseek 3Di substitution matrix measures 3Di sequence similarity during sampling-parameter selection. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: The open-closed mod-minimizer algorithm
indicators: The authors introduce the open-closed mod-minimizer algorithm to sample k-mers from DNA strings at reduced density. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: MSAProbs: multiple sequence alignment based on pair hidden Markov models and partition function posterior probabilities
indicators: Forward and Backward algorithms compute pair-HMM probabilities. Dynamic programming computes partition-function probabilities. Corresponding values are combined by root mean square. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Identification of Direct Residue Contacts in Protein–Protein Interaction by Message Passing
indicators: The authors combine covariance analysis with global statistical inference to distinguish direct residue couplings from indirect correlations. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A survey of sequence-to-graph mapping algorithms in the pangenome era
indicators: Graph dynamic programming extends Needleman–Wunsch to graph structures and Smith–Waterman to directed acyclic graphs through Partial Order Alignment. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: MAFFT: A Novel Method for Rapid Multiple Sequence Alignment Based on Fast Fourier Transform
indicators: Segment-level dynamic programming selects a consistent segment order. The resulting anchors divide the full alignment matrix into smaller regions. (PDF p. 3).
Anchors at homologous segment centers exclude parts of the dynamic programming matrix from computation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Analysis of Evolutionary Algorithms for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors analyze a general evolutionary algorithm framework for the longest common subsequence problem. The framework uses the coding of Julstrom and Hinkemeyer and three fitness functions. (PDF p. 16).
The study seeks theoretical runtime guarantees for evolutionary algorithms after earlier studies reported good empirical performance on LCS. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Maximal common subsequence algorithms
indicators: A restricted longest common subsequence need not be maximal. It can therefore fail to exclude extension into a common pattern that contains the unwanted pattern. (PDF p. 2).
The maximality checker can assess whether a restricted longest common subsequence is also maximal. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Recent Evolutions of Multiple Sequence Alignment Algorithms
indicators: The author reviews developments in multiple sequence alignment algorithms, focusing on consistency and template methods. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: MUSCLE: a multiple sequence alignment method with reduced time and space complexity
indicators: MUSCLE builds a progressive protein alignment, improves its guide tree, and applies iterative refinement. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: An nf-core framework for the systematic comparison of alternative modeling tools: the multiple sequence alignment case study
indicators: The authors present nf-core/multiplesequencealign for deploying and comparing protein multiple sequence alignment methods. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Multiple sequence alignment with the Clustal series of programs
indicators: Clustal builds a multiple alignment through successive pairwise alignments in guide-tree order. The original implementation combined progressive alignment with memory-efficient dynamic programming. (PDF p. 1).
ClustalW replaced the initial word-based comparison with dynamic programming and replaced UPGMA guide-tree construction with neighbour-joining. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Matching for Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: The authors compute an LCS directly from run-length encoded strings. The final time bound depends on run counts rather than decoded lengths. (PDF p. 2).
Find an LCS in time polynomial in the compressed input size. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Levenshtein Distance, Sequence Comparison and Biological Database Search
indicators: The authors connect Levenshtein distance, dynamic programming alignment, BLAST heuristics, and metric-based database search. (PDF p. 1).
Explain how the metric properties of edit distance support database search optimizations. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A fast homology program for aligning biological sequences
indicators: Taylor presents procedures that compute evolutionary distance and an optimal alignment path in one pass of MN iterations. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Profile Analysis: Detection of Distantly Related Proteins
indicators: The authors attribute selectivity to position-specific amino acid preferences and gap penalties. Dynamic programming places gaps under these constraints. (PDF p. 4).

PROFANAL reads replacement scores from the profile row and target-residue column. Single-sequence comparisons generally use Smith–Waterman local alignment. Database searches and dot plots use the forward/backward matrix method. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Distinct squares in run-length encoded strings
indicators: Liu proves that the number of distinct square types in the covering set is less than (14/3)N. Here, N is the number of runs in the run-length encoding. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: An Improved Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm for Reducing Memory Complexity in Global Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: SB_LCS reduces stored LCS information by reconstructing rows during traceback. It stores values that cannot be reconstructed in a stack. (PDF p. 3).
The authors report tests on DNA sequences up to 100 kb. They retain O(MN) time complexity and report lower memory use than full-table LCS. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Deep embedding and alignment of protein sequences
indicators: DEDAL combines contextual protein embeddings with Smith–Waterman local alignment. It learns substitution scores and affine gap penalties for each pair of residue positions. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Measuring the distance between multiple sequence alignments
indicators: Blackburne and Whelan introduce four metrics for comparing multiple sequence alignments. The metrics use different amounts of gap information. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Variation Graph Toolkit Improves Read Mapping by Representing Genetic Variation in the Reference
indicators: GCSA2 indexes paths to locate Maximal Exact Matches (MEMs) for seed-and-extend graph dynamic programming. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Algorithms for Computing the Longest Parameterized Common Subsequence
indicators: The authors introduce LPCS to combine four gap-constrained LCS variants in one model. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Prediction of Physical-Chemical Properties of Amino Acids from Genetic Code
indicators: The authors use the crystal basis model of the genetic code to derive relations between amino acid physical-chemical properties. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: On the Theory and Computation of Evolutionary Distances
indicators: Sellers defines evolutionary distance as the minimum total weight of mutations and deletions that make two sequences alike. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Constrained Longest Common Subsequences with Run-Length-Encoded Strings
indicators: The authors study a longest common subsequence of X and Y that contains a required string P as a subsequence. (PDF p. 1).
The method reduces dynamic programming work by computing faces of matched cuboids instead of their full surfaces. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Optimizing multiple sequence alignments using a genetic algorithm based on three objectives: structural information, non-gaps percentage and totally conserved columns
indicators: MO-SAStrE refines protein multiple sequence alignments with NSGA-II. It jointly maximizes STRIKE score, non-gap percentage and totally conserved column percentage. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: On Computing the Length of Longest Increasing Subsequences
indicators: Fredman studies the length L of a longest increasing subsequence in a sequence of n distinct, linearly ordered elements. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast, accurate construction of multiple sequence alignments from protein language embeddings
indicators: ARIES constructs protein MSAs with windowed reciprocal embedding similarity, dynamic time warping, and a synthesized template. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Accelign: a GPU-based library for accelerating pairwise sequence alignment
indicators: Accelign implements pairwise alignment on CUDA GPUs with a common DP wavefront design. It supports DNA, RNA, and protein sequences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Sassy: fuzzy searching DNA sequences using SIMD
indicators: Sassy reports all occurrences of a pattern within a text under edit distance without requiring an offline index. (PDF p. 2).
Runtime is analyzed across varying edit distance thresholds k and pattern lengths. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Improving the Worst Case Performance of the Hunt-Szymanski Strategy for the Longest Common Subsequence of Two Strings
indicators: The proposed longest common subsequence algorithm follows a schedule similar to Hunt–Szymanski while improving worst-case efficiency. (PDF p. 2).
At least one longest common subsequence uses a dominant match at every rank. Thus dominant matches suffice to solve the problem. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A General Method Applicable to the Search for Similarities in the Amino Acid Sequence of Two Proteins
indicators: The authors present a computer method to find a maximum match between two protein sequences. It permits gaps and preserves sequence order. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Codes With Run-Length and GC-Content Constraints for DNA-Based Data Storage
indicators: The authors encode binary data as DNA sequences with homopolymer runs of at most three bases. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: SAFARI: pangenome alignment of ancient DNA using
indicators: The authors develop SAFARI to align ancient DNA reads to pangenome graphs under severe post-mortem damage. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Computing a Longest Increasing Subsequence of Length k in Time O(n log log k)
indicators: The authors give a RAM algorithm that computes LIS length k in O(n log log k) time for a permutation of n integers. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Optimal alignment between groups of sequences and its application to multiple sequence alignment
indicators: Gotoh develops four dynamic programming algorithms for aligning two prealigned sequence groups with internal gaps. (PDF p. 1).
Algorithm A applies conventional dynamic programming with a uniform gap-opening penalty. It does not account for the positions of internal gaps. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Rewriting protein alphabets with language models
indicators: The authors present TEA, a 20-letter discrete structure-aware alphabet distilled from protein language models. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Compressed Dictionary Matching on Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: The authors report all occurrences of multiple patterns in a text when both inputs use run-length encoding. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast and accurate protein structure search with Foldseek
indicators: SIMD Smith–Waterman alignment combines amino acid and 3Di substitution scores with weights 1.4 and 2.1. Foldseek-TM instead applies TM-align after the initial search. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Efficient seeding for error-prone sequences with SubseqHash2
indicators: SubseqHash2 produces multiple subsequence seeds in one dynamic programming computation. It targets sequences with high error rates. (PDF p. 1).
The dynamic program first solves subproblems by recurrence. It then finds the minimum-ranked subsequence for each order and window, reusing subproblems across windows. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: End-to-end learning of multiple sequence alignments
indicators: The Learned Alignment Module constructs differentiable multiple sequence alignments with smooth Smith–Waterman. A downstream learning objective can update the alignment. (PDF p. 2).

Smooth Smith–Waterman replaces max with logsumexp and argmax with softmax. Higher-scoring paths receive greater probability, and residue-pair alignment probabilities can be expressed as derivatives. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: On Multiple Insertion-Deletion Correcting Codes
indicators: Helberg and Ferreira study binary insertion/deletion correcting codes through codeword weights, Hamming distances, and weighted moments. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Multiple protein structure alignment at scale with FoldMason
indicators: FoldMason constructs multiple protein structure alignments with a progressive algorithm that uses the Foldseek 3Di+AA alphabet. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning (Alphafold)
indicators: AlphaFold predicts residue distance distributions from sequence and multiple sequence alignment features. These distributions define a protein-specific structural potential. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Characterization of pairwise and multiple sequence alignment errors
indicators: The authors compare simulated true alignments with ALIGN pairwise alignments and ClustalW multiple sequence alignments. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold
indicators: AlphaFold predicts protein atomic coordinates with a neural network that uses sequence, MSA, and structural information. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Algorithms for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: Hirschberg presents two algorithms that recover an LCS. Their time bounds depend on the LCS length p for input lengths m ≤ n. (PDF p. 1).
Recover an LCS with input-dependent bounds that can be below quadratic time. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast and exact gap-affine partial order alignment
indicators: The authors argue that SIMD accelerates full dynamic programming without removing its memory demand. Adaptive banding reduces computation but loses the optimality guarantee. (PDF p. 2).
High sequence diversity reduces exact-match runs and can make POASTA slower than SPOA. A* also has less predictable memory access than contiguous dynamic programming. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Bit-parallel sequence-to-graph alignment
indicators: Find a graph path with minimum edit distance to the complete query. Mismatches, insertions, and deletions have unit cost. (PDF p. 2).
The alignment DP uses one column per graph node and one row per query character. Its recurrence considers matches or mismatches, deletions, and insertions. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Sequential and Parallel Algorithms for the All-Substrings Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present sequential and parallel algorithms for the all-substrings longest common subsequence problem. (PDF p. 2).
The algorithm computes LCS lengths for all substrings of one string against another using Monge matrix properties. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Algorithms for approximate string matching
indicators: Ukkonen develops edit-distance algorithms whose cost depends on the edit distance s and string lengths m and n. The reported time bound is O(s min(m,n)). (PDF p. 1).
The approach reduces unnecessary dynamic-programming work when the edit distance is small. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A theoretical model for whole genome alignment
indicators: The report is part of the sequence-alignment literature corpus.

papers.title: MacCorles: Minimum Alignment Cost Computation on Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: The authors compute an LCS alignment that first maximizes equal character pairs and then minimizes insertions and deletions. (PDF p. 1).
An LCS length alone does not distinguish alignments with different gap counts. The DNA example has two LCS choices, but only the AA choice permits a gap-free alignment. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Efficient mapping of accurate long reads in minimizer space with mapquik
indicators: mapquik maps accurate long reads with seeds made from k consecutive sampled minimizers. It indexes only seeds that occur once in the reference. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BLAT—The BLAST-Like Alignment Tool
indicators: Hit sorting takes O(N log N) time in the stated analysis. HSP chaining uses O(N²) dynamic programming, where N is the HSP count. (PDF p. 8).
Protein alignment extends seeds into ungapped HSPs with match score +2 and mismatch score −1. A weighted HSP graph and dynamic programming select the highest-scoring chain. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Pangenome graph construction from genome alignments with Minigraph-Cactus
indicators: Minigraph-Cactus constructs pangenome graphs directly from genome assemblies. The authors demonstrate construction with 90 human haplotypes and with Drosophila melanogaster. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: On Computing Average Common Substring Over Run Length Encoded Sequences
indicators: ACS averages the longest match between each suffix of X and any suffix of Y. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Construction of Phylogenetic Trees Walter
indicators: The authors present a method to reconstruct phylogenetic trees from amino acid sequence differences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Robust Deep Learning–Based Protein Sequence Design Using ProteinMPNN
indicators: The authors introduce ProteinMPNN, a deep learning model for de novo protein sequence design on target backbones. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Coarse-Grained Parallel Algorithm for the All-Substrings Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present a BSP/CGM parallel algorithm for all-substrings longest common subsequence (ALCS). It computes LCS lengths for A and every substring of B. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm also reconstructs an actual longest common subsequence of A and B. (PDF p. 32).

papers.title: T-Coffee: A Novel Method for Fast and Accurate Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: The authors introduce T-Coffee for progressive multiple sequence alignment with reduced greedy error accumulation. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Geometric algebra generation of molecular surfaces
indicators: The authors generate molecular surfaces with a Clifford–Fourier transform (CFT) and a PDE transform. They test piecewise and Gaussian initial data. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Haplotype-aware sequence alignment to pangenome graphs
indicators: A Minichain implementation improves agreement with simulated recombinations and real CHM13 haplotypes. The implemented contribution is chaining; the new base-level alignment algorithm remains future work. (PDF p. 8).
Haplotype paths form a path cover for sparse dynamic programming. Preprocessing records the last vertex on each haplotype path that can reach each graph vertex. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Fast discrete convolution in R2 with radial kernels using non-uniform fast Fourier transform with nonequispaced frequencies
indicators: The method computes discrete convolutions with radial kernels in two dimensions. Its Fourier frequencies lie on concentric circles. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: GPU-accelerated homology search with MMseqs2
indicators: The gapless recurrence is M[i,j] = max(M[i−1,j−1] + Q[i,sj], 0). Zero boundary values permit local alignment. The maximum matrix value gives the optimal gapless score. (PDF p. 5).
Each reference sequence is aligned against a query PSSM. The top k sequences that pass the inclusion threshold proceed to profile-based Smith–Waterman–Gotoh alignment on the GPU. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: A Faster Algorithm Computing String Edit Distances
indicators: The algorithm can produce an optimal edit sequence. Longest common subsequence computation is a special case. (PDF p. 1).
The baseline recurrence takes the minimum cost of replacement, deletion, or insertion from three adjacent matrix entries. Each entry takes constant time, giving O(|A||B|) time. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Efficient algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem with sequential substring constraints
indicators: SSCLCS seeks a longest common subsequence that contains specified strings as substrings in a fixed order. (PDF p. 2).
The non-overlapping correctness proof separates ordinary LCS extensions from completion of a constraint. Invalid or incomplete constraint states retain the value −∞. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Computing the longest topological common subsequence of a symbol-wise totally ordered directed acyclic graph and a sequence
indicators: Find a longest common subsequence of B and any sequence specified by a topological sort of G. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Linear-space S-table algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem
indicators: The authors develop algorithms for concatenated LCS, S-table merging, and incremental character updates using linear-space S-tables. (PDF p. 2).
Compute LCS lengths for concatenated strings and updated strings while retaining the linear-space representation. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: The design and construction of reference pangenome graphs with minigraph
indicators: The authors develop minigraph for the incremental construction and alignment of reference pangenome graphs. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Protein Secondary Structure Prediction Based on Position-Specific Scoring Matrices
indicators: PSIPRED predicts secondary structure with two neural networks. Its input is the position-specific scoring matrix generated by PSI-BLAST. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: QuickEd: high-performance exact sequence alignment based on bound-and-align
indicators: QuickEd first estimates an upper bound on edit distance. It then uses that bound to restrict DP computation and recover an optimal alignment. (PDF p. 2).
The implementation supports only edit distance. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Nomenclature for incompletely specified bases in nucleic acid sequences: recommendations 1984
indicators: The recommendations assign single-letter symbols to sets of possible bases at a sequence position. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Protein embeddings and local alignments
indicators: E-score computes local alignments by dynamic programming with affine gap penalties. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: CREMSA: compressed indexing of (ultra) large multiple sequence alignments
indicators: CREMSA compresses multiple sequence alignments by column runs and supports queries without full decompression. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Different Longest Common Subsequence Algorithms
indicators: The authors compare LCS algorithms through their computation methods and stated time and space costs. (PDF p. 1).
The comparison covers dynamic programming, divide and conquer, match-point processing, and diagonal edit-graph traversal. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A new approach to regular & indeterminate strings
indicators: The authors define string regularity through transitive matching among positions. A regular string can contain letters with multiple characters. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (Unless SETH is False)
indicators: Backurs and Indyk show that strongly subquadratic exact edit distance would refute SETH. (PDF p. 1).
This version reduces orthogonal vectors to edit distance over an alphabet of four symbols. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Direct-Coupling Analysis of Residue Coevolution Captures Native Contacts Across Many Protein Families
indicators: Mean-field direct-coupling analysis, or mfDCA, predicts residue contacts from multiple-sequence alignments by separating direct from indirect correlations. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Building pangenome graphs
indicators: PGGB builds pangenome variation graphs through all-to-all alignment, graph induction, and local graph normalization. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Rapid, accurate long- and short-read mapping to large pangenome graphs with vg Giraffe
indicators: Candidate chains are aligned using base-level graph dynamic programming. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Binary Codes Capable of Correcting Deletions, Insertions, and Reversals
indicators: The report is part of the sequence-alignment literature corpus.

papers.title: Amino Acid Substitution Matrices from Protein Blocks
indicators: The authors derive BLOSUM substitution matrices from residue pairs in conserved, ungapped protein blocks. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Methods for Assessing the Statistical Significance of Molecular Sequence Features by Using General Scoring Schemes
indicators: The authors derive statistical formulas for high segment scores under general scoring schemes. They also describe the composition of high-scoring segments. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Efficient merged longest common subsequence algorithms for similar sequences
indicators: The authors present merged longest common subsequence algorithms for similar sequences. The merge preserves the order of characters taken from each input sequence. (PDF p. 2).

The authors contrast their goal with earlier algorithms that perform well when the answer length is small. They use the diagonal concept from an earlier LCS algorithm to address similar inputs. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improving spliced alignment by modeling splice sites with deep learning
indicators: Minimap2 incorporates donor and acceptor scores in its spliced dynamic programming recurrence. Miniprot uses the same score functions in a more complex recurrence. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Edit distance for a run-length-encoded string and an uncompressed string
indicators: The authors aim to compute edit distance directly from one compressed string. The computation depends on its run count rather than its full length. (PDF p. 2).
A run-level recurrence splits the uncompressed prefix at position u. It combines the previous run-row value with the distance between the current run and the remaining substring. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A fast algorithm for finding the positions of all squares in a run-length encoded string
indicators: The authors present Algorithm SQUARES to locate square occurrences directly in a run-length encoded string with N runs. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: An O(ND) Difference Algorithm and Its Variations
indicators: Myers relates longest common subsequences and shortest insertion-deletion scripts to paths in an edit graph. (PDF p. 1).
A shortest-path view explains the connection between LCS and edit scripts. A specialized Dijkstra algorithm has the same time order but requires more complex queue management. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Functional protein mining with conformal guarantees
indicators: The authors calibrate protein retrieval thresholds to control a selected loss at a user-defined risk level. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: PLMSearch: Protein language model powers accurate and fast sequence search for remote homology
indicators: PLMAlign calculates residue substitution scores with dot products. It uses Smith–Waterman or Needleman–Wunsch with a linear gap penalty. The main experiments use global alignment scores. (PDF p. 7).
The pipeline also provides optional sequence-based Needleman–Wunsch alignment and structure-based TM-align for retrieved pairs. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: AlphaFold and Implications for Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
indicators: The authors examine how to interpret AlphaFold regions with low confidence that overlap intrinsically disordered regions. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An Evolutionary Model for Maximum Likelihood Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: The authors derive maximum likelihood alignment of two DNA sequences from a statistical model with explicit transition probabilities. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Gap Costs for Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: Quasi-natural gap costs approximate natural gap costs while reducing the alignment history needed by dynamic programming. (PDF p. 12).
Quasi-natural costs reduce the number of histories needed to evaluate gap costs during dynamic programming. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: A Linear Space Algorithm for Computing Maximal Common Subsequences
indicators: Hirschberg presents an algorithm that constructs a longest common subsequence in quadratic time and linear space. (PDF p. 1).
The method combines row-based dynamic programming with recursive division into smaller string-pair problems. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Unifying Look at Data Structures
indicators: Vuillemin uses geometrical combinatorics to derive data structures and algorithms for searching and list manipulation. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: On the Economical Construction of the Transitive Closure of a Directed Graph
indicators: The authors construct the transitive closure of an acyclic directed graph in O(n³/ln n) operations. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Basic Local Alignment Search Tool
indicators: The report is part of the sequence-alignment literature corpus.

papers.title: Accurate Structure Prediction of Biomolecular Interactions with AlphaFold 3
indicators: AlphaFold 3 predicts joint structures containing proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, and modified residues. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An almost-linear time and linear space algorithm for the longest common subsequence problem
indicators: The authors present a primal-dual LCS implementation with O(nL) time and claimed O(n) space. L is the LCS length, and both input lengths are O(n). (PDF p. 2).
The primal-dual procedure assigns each matching pair to the first compatible conjugate-order set. The number of sets gives the LCS length. Predecessor links recover an LCS. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and accurate multiple-protein-sequence alignment at scale with FAMSA2
indicators: FAMSA2 uses a longest common subsequence dissimilarity measure designed to tolerate sequence divergence. It also refines partial alignments during progressive alignment. (PDF p. 2).
Length-based prefiltering reduces pairwise comparisons. Parallel execution operates within LCS calculation and progressive alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming on DAGs with Small Width
indicators: The authors formulate sparse dynamic programming and co-linear chaining on directed acyclic graphs parameterized by path width. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Protein Homology Detection by HMM–HMM Comparison
indicators: HHsearch uses Viterbi dynamic programming to find the HMM alignment path with the maximum log-sum-of-odds score. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Parasail: SIMD C Library for Global, Semi-Global, and Local Pairwise Sequence Alignments
indicators: Parasail is a C99 SIMD library for Smith-Waterman, Needleman-Wunsch, and semi-global pairwise alignment. (PDF p. 2).
Dynamic programming provides an optimal alignment for a specified scoring function. The author contrasts this guarantee with heuristics that can return suboptimal alignments. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Chirality in a quaternionic representation of the genetic code
indicators: The authors extend a quaternionic genetic-code representation to include chirality. Conjugate quaternions represent the two chiral systems. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A flexible multiple sequence alignment program
indicators: The program also provides Needleman–Wunsch dynamic programming for pairwise alignment. (PDF p. 2).
Dynamic programming selects non-overlapping region paths that maximize S = aL − bD. L is total region length, D is total intervening deletions, and both weights default to one. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Diagnosing protein sequence search in the era of language
indicators: PLM-GUARD tests whether protein search scores support biological interpretation. It contains six checks across biological fidelity, semantic validity, and manipulation safety. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming I: Linear Cost Functions
indicators: The authors introduce sparse dynamic programming algorithms for sequence alignment and RNA structure with linear gap costs. (PDF p. 1).
Exploit sparsity in dynamic programming recurrences when the number of candidate match points M is much less than n^2. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Accurate multiple alignment of distantly related genome sequences using filtered spaced word matches as anchor points
indicators: The authors use filtered spaced-word matches to generate anchors for genome alignment. They extend selected matches with an X-drop algorithm. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (Unless SETH is False)
indicators: The authors seek evidence that the known near-quadratic bounds for exact edit distance are tight. (PDF p. 1).
Edit distance adds costs across aligned gadgets. Thus, every nonorthogonal vector pair must have the same gadget cost, independent of the number of shared 1s. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: On the Complexity of Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: Jain and colleagues study sequence-to-graph alignment under Hamming and edit distance. They distinguish changes to the query, graph labels, or both. (PDF p. 1).

Table 1 compares asymptotic running times with prior algorithms for edit distance, arbitrary linear costs, and affine gaps. The new bound matches the listed best edit-distance bound and improves the listed bounds for the other two settings. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and Accurate Short Read Alignment with Burrows–Wheeler Transform
indicators: Paired-end mapping sorts candidate coordinates and scans them to form pairs. Smith–Waterman alignment rescues unmapped reads whose mates map reliably. (PDF p. 4).
For SOLiD reads, BWA searches a color-space reference index. Dynamic programming then decodes mapped reads into nucleotide sequences. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Minimap2: Pairwise Alignment for Nucleotide Sequences
indicators: The Suzuki–Kasahara recurrence stores score differences bounded by scoring parameters. Suitable parameter bounds permit 8-bit values and 16-way SSE vectorization regardless of peak alignment score. (PDF p. 3).
Index reference minimizers in a hash table. Find query anchors, chain colinear anchors with dynamic programming, and align between anchors and beyond chain ends. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: MMseqs2 searches protein sequence sets through k-mer filtering, ungapped alignment, and vectorized Smith–Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 1).
The authors report that k-mer filtering removes 99.9% of targets and ungapped filtering removes a further 99%. About 10⁻⁵ of targets reach Smith–Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Block-Sorting Lossless Data Compression Algorithm
indicators: The algorithm applies a reversible transformation to an input block. Sorting groups characters by context and makes redundancy easier for simple coders to use. (PDF p. 22).

papers.title: A Model of Evolutionary Change in Proteins
indicators: The authors derive amino acid replacement matrices from 1,572 accepted point mutations in 71 groups of closely related proteins. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: HPRC2: A human pangenome reference with near-complete coverage of common genetic variation
indicators: The authors present HPRC2 with 460 haplotypes, three pangenome alignment representations, and matched transcriptome and epigenome data. (PDF p. 35).

papers.title: Theseus: fast and optimal affine-gap sequence-tograph alignment
indicators: The authors introduce Theseus, a sequence-to-graph aligner based on wavefront alignment (WFA) with affine gap costs. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Fast and Practical Bit-Vector Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present a bit-vector algorithm for LCS length with O(nm/w) time and O(m/w) space, where m ≤ n and w is the machine word size. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm processes dynamic programming columns through word-level parallelism. For m ≤ w, the authors give linear time and constant additional working space. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: MAFFT version 5: improvement in accuracy of multiple sequence alignment
indicators: G-INS-i uses global pairwise alignments with an FFT approximation. H-INS-i uses FASTA with Smith–Waterman optimization. F-INS-i uses FASTA without that optimization. (PDF p. 3).
Dynamic programming aligns groups using substitution scores and importance values. Iterative refinement then optimizes the WSP+I objective. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Gapped BLAST and PSI-BLAST: A New Generation of Protein Database Search Programs
indicators: Gapped extension uses dynamic programming in both directions from a seed. It retains cells whose optimal local score is no more than Xg below the best score found. (PDF p. 5).
The Xg rule adapts the dynamic programming region to the data. An alignment can cross many diagonals while the active region in each row remains limited. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Exact global alignment using A* with chaining seed heuristic and match pruning
indicators: A*PA computes exact global pairwise alignment under unit edit costs with A* search. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Solving longest common subsequence problems via a transformation to the maximum clique problem
indicators: The authors transform constrained LCS problems into instances of the maximum clique problem. (PDF p. 2).
Exact and heuristic maximum clique solvers are applied to solve repetition-free and arc-preserving LCS variants. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Deep reinforcement learning-based pairwise DNA sequence alignment method compatible with embedded edge devices
indicators: EdgeAlign uses a dueling deep Q-network to align DNA sequences through a fixed sliding window. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and sensitive multiple sequence alignments on a microcomputer
indicators: CLUSTAL4 progressively aligns sequence groups in the branching order of an initial dendrogram. It preserves gaps from earlier alignment stages. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: The Physical Origin of Intrinsic Bends in Double Helical DNA
indicators: The authors investigate the physical origin of intrinsic DNA curvature in phased A-tracts using molecular dynamics. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Rapid and sensitive protein complex alignment with Foldseek-Multimer
indicators: The authors develop Foldseek-Multimer to align multimeric protein complexes at high speed. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Hidden Markov Models in Computational Biology: Applications to Protein Modeling
indicators: The authors train HMMs on unaligned sequences to model globins, kinase catalytic domains, and EF-hand motifs. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast Optimal Alignment
indicators: Reduce the cost of Needleman–Wunsch-type alignment while retaining an optimal result. (PDF p. 3).
The base recurrence selects the minimum cost from insertion, deletion, and match or mismatch predecessors. A path matrix records the selected transitions. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Improvement in accuracy of multiple sequence alignment using novel group-to-group sequence alignment algorithm with piecewise linear gap cost
indicators: An insertion length profile stores information for each group column. Dynamic gap information tracks gaps inserted during dynamic programming. (PDF p. 2).
PRIME optimizes a weighted sum-of-pairs objective with a simpler dynamic programming method. It omits candidate lists and anchoring heuristics. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: The CLUSTAL_X windows interface: flexible strategies for multiple sequence alignment aided by quality analysis tools
indicators: The authors introduce CLUSTAL_X, a graphical user interface for the ClustalW multiple sequence alignment engine. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast, Scalable Generation of High-Quality Protein Multiple Sequence Alignments Using Clustal Omega
indicators: Clustal Omega combines a scalable guide tree method with profile HMM alignment to construct protein MSAs. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A New Bucket-Based Algorithm for Finding LCS from two given Molecular Sequences
indicators: The method aims to find an LCS while preparing the permanently stored database sequence only once. (PDF p. 1).
The procedure writes selected nucleotides to an LCS array, flags bucket entries, updates Ptr, and deletes queue entries according to Mark. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: The Z curve database: a graphic representation of genome sequences
indicators: The authors present the Z curve database, providing three-dimensional geometric representations of genome sequences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast Gap-Affine Pairwise Alignment Using the Wavefront Algorithm
indicators: WFA computes exact global pairwise alignments with gap-affine penalties. It advances partial alignments in increasing score order. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improved Tools for Biological Sequence Comparison
indicators: FASTA joins compatible regions of sequence similarity to improve database search sensitivity. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A Relative Position based Algorithm to find out the Longest Common Subsequence from Multiple Biological Sequences
indicators: Reported length ratios exceed 97% in the listed tests. These results do not show exact LCS recovery in every case. (PDF p. 6).
The authors show a three-sequence example where the compared Rizvi–Agarwal heuristic returns TAT of length three. They identify ATAT of length four as an LCS. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Faster algorithms for RNA-folding using the Four-Russians method
indicators: The recurrence compares an endpoint-pair solution with all split-point solutions. Only A–U and C–G pairs contribute to the matching count. (PDF p. 3).
The main algorithm processes complete groups with table lookups. At most 2q residual terms per cell use the original recurrence. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Algorithms for Two Versions of LCS Problem for Indeterminate Strings
indicators: The authors study LCS for indeterminate strings, where each position contains a nonempty set of symbols. Two positions match when their sets intersect. (PDF p. 3).
Precomputed match tables let dynamic programming algorithms for standard strings use constant-time tests for indeterminate matches. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Recognition and Complexity of Point Visibility Graphs
indicators: The authors investigate the computational complexity of recognizing point visibility graphs in the Euclidean plane. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Fast and accurate de novo genome assembly from long uncorrected reads
indicators: Racon generates consensus sequences from raw reads, backbone sequences, and mappings. It uses SIMD-accelerated partial-order alignment. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Quantum Groups and the Genetic Code
indicators: The authors propose Uq(sl(2) ⊕ sl(2)) at q approaching zero as a symmetry model for the genetic code. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An Improved Algorithm for Matching Biological Sequences
indicators: P(m,n) = min(D(m−1,n) + w(1), P(m−1,n) + u). Q uses the corresponding recurrence along the other sequence. (PDF p. 2).
The derived recurrence reduces the stated computational order from M²N to MN for the specified gap-cost form. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Profile Hidden Markov Models
indicators: Profile HMMs convert multiple sequence alignments into probabilistic scoring models for remote homology searches. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Alignment of Whole Genomes
indicators: The system aligns small polymorphic gaps with dynamic programming equivalent to Smith–Waterman. This gives an optimal local alignment under specified insertion and mutation costs. (PDF p. 5).
Unique exact matches divide the alignment into smaller gap problems. This limits the regions that require Smith–Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: An Analysis on Computation of Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm
indicators: The authors compare LCS algorithms for two strings and multiple strings, with emphasis on time and memory requirements. (PDF p. 1).
The review separates dynamic programming methods into row-by-row, contour-to-contour, and diagonal-wise procedures according to which table cells they process. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
indicators: LoL-align iteratively optimizes a local log-odds score for protein structure alignment. The score uses intramolecular Cα distances and sequence distances. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Speeding-up Hirschberg and Hunt-Szymanski LCS Algorithms
indicators: The authors present bit-parallel formulations of the Hirschberg and Hunt-Szymanski LCS algorithms. (PDF p. 1).
Accelerate classic longest common subsequence algorithms by exploiting word-level parallelism. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Matching Sequences under Deletion/Insertion Constraints
indicators: Find a longest common subsequence subject to a bound on its deletion/insertion index. (PDF p. 2).
The author states that the proposed constraint cannot be expressed through the cell weights and gap penalties of the Needleman–Wunsch method. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: TM-Vec 2: Accelerated Protein Homology Detection for Structural Similarity
indicators: The authors introduce TM-Vec 2 and TM-Vec 2s for fast protein structural similarity prediction from sequence alone. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: M2Align: parallel multiple sequence alignment with a multi-objective metaheuristic
indicators: M2Align reimplements MO-SAStrE in Java using NSGA-II. It optimizes STRIKE, totally conserved columns, and non-gap percentage together. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Heaviest Increasing-Common Subsequence Problems
indicators: The authors define heaviest increasing subsequence (HIS) and heaviest common subsequence (HCS) problems as weighted extensions of LIS and LCS. (PDF p. 1).
The minimal distance LCS problem supports screen updates. It selects an LCS that minimizes the total displacement of matched lines. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Bounded Weighted Edit Distance
indicators: The authors give a dynamic algorithm for bounded weighted edit distance with arbitrary normalized edit costs. A fixed threshold k controls preprocessing and update costs. (PDF p. 1).
Determine how quickly weighted edit distance can be maintained when strings change and the distance is small. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Optimal Alignments in Linear Space
indicators: The cost-only algorithm updates two row vectors in place. Three scalar values retain the insertion state and adjacent costs needed by the recurrence. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Finding the longest common subsequence for multiple biological sequences by ant colony optimization
indicators: The authors propose ant colony optimization (ACO) to find approximate longest common subsequences for multiple biological sequences. (PDF p. 1).
The authors motivate heuristic search through the NP-hardness of the general problem and the O(l^n) cost of dynamic programming for n sequences of length l. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Differentiable Alignment Framework for Sequence-to-Sequence Modeling via Optimal Transport
indicators: The authors introduce Sequence Optimal Transport Distance (SOTD), a sequence pseudo-metric based on differentiable one-dimensional optimal transport. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: ProbCons: Probabilistic Consistency-Based Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: Needleman–Wunsch maximizes the sum of match posterior probabilities with zero gap penalties. Expected accuracy divides this sum by the shorter sequence length. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: The synergy between protein positioning and DNA elasticity: energy minimization of protein-decorated DNA minicircles
indicators: The authors model protein-decorated DNA minicircles using base-pair level elastic energy minimization. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming II: Convex and Concave Cost Functions
indicators: The authors extend sparse dynamic programming to non-linear, convex, and concave gap cost functions. (PDF p. 1).
Generalize sparse dynamic programming to non-linear cost functions without incurring full quadratic overhead. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Mugsy: fast multiple alignment of closely related whole genomes
indicators: Mugsy aligns closely related whole genomes without a reference genome. It accepts mixtures of complete genomes and assembled draft genomes. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Muscle5: High-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased assessments of sequence homology and phylogeny
indicators: Muscle5 generates ensembles of accurate multiple sequence alignments by changing HMM parameters and guide-tree joining order. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: HHblits: Lightning-Fast Iterative Protein Sequence Searching by HMM–HMM Alignment
indicators: The prefilter first uses ungapped local alignment. It then uses Smith–Waterman alignment with affine gap costs of 5 bits for opening and 1 bit for extension. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Protein structure alignment by Reseek improves sensitivity to remote homologs
indicators: Residue-pair scores sum weighted feature log-odds scores. Smith–Waterman or a BLAST-like method constructs local alignments with affine gap penalties. The default representation combines amino acid type with eight 16-letter structural features. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: COFFEE: an objective function for multiple sequence alignments
indicators: COFFEE scores a multiple sequence alignment by its consistency with a library of pairwise alignments. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Evaluating the significance of embedding-based protein sequence alignment with clustering and double dynamic programming for remote homology
indicators: The authors refine protein residue embedding similarities with Z-score normalization, K-means clustering, and two dynamic programming alignments. (PDF p. 2).
A first Needleman–Wunsch alignment uses zero gap penalties. K-means groups the combined residue embeddings from both sequences into 20 clusters. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Identification of Common Molecular Subsequences
indicators: The authors give a matrix algorithm to find the most similar segment pair in two molecular sequences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Ultrafast and Memory-Efficient Alignment of Short DNA Sequences to the Human Genome
indicators: The authors introduce Bowtie, an ultrafast short-read aligner based on the Burrows-Wheeler transform (BWT). (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An Icelandic pangenome reference
indicators: The authors introduce Emblask for hybrid haplotype assembly and Weaver for short-read mapping to pangenomes. Their goal is to reduce reference bias. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming for Longest Common Subsequence from Fragments
indicators: The authors present sparse dynamic programming algorithms for computing the LCS from fragment matches. (PDF p. 1).
Efficiently compute longest common subsequences on long strings when matching substrings are sparse. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Efficient CGM-based parallel algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem with multiple substring-exclusion constraints
indicators: The authors parallelize LCS computation with multiple forbidden substrings. They use Wang et al.'s dynamic programming algorithm as the sequential basis. (PDF p. 2).
The task DAG groups automaton-state subproblems at each input-position pair. Its edges represent the dependencies of the dynamic programming recurrence. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Protein 3D Structure Computed from Evolutionary Sequence Variation
indicators: EVfold infers residue couplings from multiple sequence alignments with a maximum entropy model. It converts these couplings into distance constraints for protein structure generation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Opportunistic Data Structures with Applications
indicators: The authors combine Burrows–Wheeler compression with suffix arrays to support searches in compressed text. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: String editing under pattern constraints
indicators: Dynamic programming traverses cross-product graphs between input string positions and regular expression automata. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: A Review on Sequence Alignment Algorithms for Short Reads Based on Next-Generation Sequencing
indicators: FASTA selects k-tuple matches, scores candidate regions, and applies Smith–Waterman alignment. Its score threshold can exclude valid alignments. (PDF p. 3).
BFAST builds reference indexes, applies masks to obtain spaced seeds, and identifies candidate alignment locations. It then applies Smith–Waterman local alignment. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Protein embedding based alignment
indicators: PEbA uses contextual residue embeddings to score pairwise protein alignments. It applies dynamic programming similar to Smith-Waterman. (PDF p. 3).
The authors propose integrating the score into faster dynamic programming implementations. This is a proposed improvement. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: A draft human pangenome reference
indicators: The authors present a draft human pangenome based on 47 phased diploid assemblies from genetically diverse individuals. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Automated assembly of protein blocks for database searching
indicators: PROTOMAT automatically finds conserved ungapped protein alignments and assembles them into compatible block sets for database searches. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Efficient algorithms for the longest common subsequence in k-length substrings
indicators: They give dynamic programming, sparse, dense, and tabulation algorithms. All use linear-time preprocessing to find matching length-k substrings. (PDF p. 1).
The authors aim to obtain O(n²) time without a constant-k restriction and to improve this bound with techniques adapted from LCS algorithms. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Label-guided seed-chain-extend alignment on annotated De Bruijn graphs
indicators: Multi-label alignment adds label changes and node length changes to alignment scoring on annotated De Bruijn graphs. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Lossless pangenome indexing using tag arrays
indicators: The method adds run-length-compressed graph-coordinate tags to an FM-index of haplotypes. Queries report distinct matching graph positions. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Iterative Coding Scheme Satisfying GC Balance and Run-Length Constraints for DNA Storage With Robustness to Error Propagation
indicators: The authors propose iterative DNA encoding with randomization, M-ary mapping, and constraint verification. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: GraphAligner: Rapid and Versatile Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: GraphAligner aligns long reads to sequence graphs with a seed-and-extend method and bit-parallel banded dynamic programming. (PDF p. 9).
The authors argue that full dynamic programming is unsuitable for aligning many reads to large graphs, even with their earlier bit-parallel acceleration. (PDF p. 2).

themes.scope_note: Shared baseline for the indexed collection. Its presence locates the report in the sequence-alignment computational landscape; it does not claim that every paper introduces a new foundational result.

papers.title: Protein remote homology detection and structural alignment using deep learning
indicators: Held-out CATH pairs and domains each had median TM-score prediction error of 0.023. Their correlations with reference scores were 0.936 and 0.901, respectively. (PDF p. 3).
DeepBLAST had lower alignment F1 scores than the tested structural methods. Its TM-score trend on Malidup was similar to Mammoth, but its prediction errors had higher variance. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: TM-align: A Protein Structure Alignment Algorithm Based on the TM-score
indicators: The authors present TM-align, a protein structure alignment algorithm that optimizes TM-score rather than RMSD. (PDF p. 1).
TM-score weights smaller residue distances stronger than larger distances, making it sensitive to global fold topology. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: The String-to-String Correction Problem
indicators: Edit distance is defined as the minimum-cost sequence of character insertions, deletions, and substitutions. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: pLM-BLAST: distant homology detection based on direct
indicators: Residue similarity depends on sequence context because scores come from embeddings rather than a fixed substitution matrix. (PDF p. 2).
The method normalizes each residue embedding by its Euclidean norm. Pairwise cosine similarities form a sequence-specific substitution matrix. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast, sensitive detection of protein homologs using deep dense retrieval
indicators: Across SCOPe queries, average TM-score decreases and average structural RMSD increases as DHR rank becomes worse. The authors interpret this as evidence of structural information in the embeddings. (PDF p. 4).
Average MSA log Meff and average structure TM-score increase together across tested configurations. The authors caution that this relation does not explain every protein case. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Accurate Prediction of Protein Structures and Interactions Using a Three-Track Neural Network
indicators: Complex tests use paired alignments for known structures with two or three chains and assess predictions with TM-score. (PDF p. 8).
Many tested complex models achieve TM-score above 0.8. Complex prediction takes about 30 minutes on a 24 GB TITAN RTX GPU. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Optimal Gap-Affine Alignment in O(s) Space
indicators: The authors present bidirectional wavefront alignment (BiWFA). It computes optimal gap-affine alignments in O(ns) time and O(s) memory, excluding input storage. Here, n is sequence length and s is the optimal alignment score. (PDF p. 2).

The authors propose extensions to edit distance, linear gaps, piecewise gap-affine penalties and semi-global alignment. These are stated extensions, rather than benchmarked applications in the excerpts. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: A*PA2: Up to 19× Faster Exact Global Alignment
indicators: A*PA2 computes exact global pairwise alignments under edit distance. It combines band doubling, bitpacking, block computation, and A* heuristics. (PDF p. 1).
Each dataset is sorted by edit distance and divided into 50 files. Reported runtimes average the sequence pairs within each file. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: Edit Distance in Near-Linear Time: it’s a Constant Factor
indicators: The authors present a randomized constant-factor approximation for edit distance. For each fixed ε > 0, its running time is O(n^(1+ε)). (PDF p. 3).
The algorithm builds distance oracles across increasing substring lengths. These oracles approximate substring distances in an average sense sufficient to estimate the full edit distance. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Bilingual language model for protein sequence and structure
indicators: Global Needleman–Wunsch alignment with the Foldseek 3Di substitution matrix measures 3Di sequence similarity during sampling-parameter selection. (PDF p. 5).
Inverse-folding tests compare ESMFold structures of generated sequences with native AlphaFold2 predictions. Metrics include lDDT, RMSD, and TM-score, with bootstrap confidence intervals. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: An nf-core framework for the systematic comparison of alternative modeling tools: the multiple sequence alignment case study
indicators: M-Coffee builds a consensus from pairwise projections of input alignments. It uses these projections in a consistency-based scoring scheme for progressive alignment. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Levenshtein Distance, Sequence Comparison and Biological Database Search
indicators: Explain how the metric properties of edit distance support database search optimizations. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Deep embedding and alignment of protein sequences
indicators: The authors argue that fixed substitution scores and uniform gap penalties restrict alignment accuracy. No single substitution matrix works well for all protein pairs. (PDF p. 2).
Restricting substitution scores to amino acid identity caused a large performance decline. Results approached those of the best fixed substitution matrix. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Sassy: fuzzy searching DNA sequences using SIMD
indicators: Sassy reports all occurrences of a pattern within a text under edit distance without requiring an offline index. (PDF p. 2).
Runtime is analyzed across varying edit distance thresholds k and pattern lengths. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: A General Method Applicable to the Search for Similarities in the Amino Acid Sequence of Two Proteins
indicators: The authors compare real protein scores with scores from shuffled sequences to assess statistical significance. (PDF p. 6).
The simplest scoring scheme assigns one to identical residue pairs and zero to other pairs. More general scores can use protein composition, codons, or neighboring cells. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and accurate protein structure search with Foldseek
indicators: Hit ranking multiplies the alignment bit score by the geometric mean of alignment LDDT and TM-score. Reverse-query score subtraction and composition correction suppress false positives. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold
indicators: Predicted confidence correlated with measured accuracy on 10,795 chains. Pearson correlations were 0.76 for pLDDT versus lDDT-Cα and 0.85 for pTM versus TM-score. (PDF p. 3).
A prediction made after CASP reproduced domain packing in a 2,180-residue chain, with r.m.s.d.95 of 2.2 Å and TM-score of 0.96. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Bit-parallel sequence-to-graph alignment
indicators: Find a graph path with minimum edit distance to the complete query. Mismatches, insertions, and deletions have unit cost. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Algorithms for approximate string matching
indicators: Ukkonen develops edit-distance algorithms whose cost depends on the edit distance s and string lengths m and n. The reported time bound is O(s min(m,n)). (PDF p. 1).
The approach reduces unnecessary dynamic-programming work when the edit distance is small. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Faster Algorithm Computing String Edit Distances
indicators: Edit distance is the minimum total cost over edit sequences that transform one string into the other. Each operation has a nonnegative cost. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: QuickEd: high-performance exact sequence alignment based on bound-and-align
indicators: QuickEd first estimates an upper bound on edit distance. It then uses that bound to restrict DP computation and recover an optimal alignment. (PDF p. 2).
QuickEd-Bound combines WindowEd with small and large windows and BandEd in a cascade to estimate the alignment score. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (Unless SETH is False)
indicators: Backurs and Indyk show that strongly subquadratic exact edit distance would refute SETH. (PDF p. 1).
This version reduces orthogonal vectors to edit distance over an alphabet of four symbols. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Edit distance for a run-length-encoded string and an uncompressed string
indicators: The authors aim to compute edit distance directly from one compressed string. The computation depends on its run count rather than its full length. (PDF p. 2).
Theorem 1 states that Algorithm 3 computes the edit distance between the RLE and uncompressed inputs in O(Mn) time. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: PLMSearch: Protein language model powers accurate and fast sequence search for remote homology
indicators: The remote homology analysis defines remote pairs by sequence identity below 0.3 and TM-score above 0.5. It compares recalled and missed pairs using these two measures. (PDF p. 4).
The authors report stronger correlation with TM-score for SS-predictor than for direct embedding similarity measures. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Diagnosing protein sequence search in the era of language
indicators: Structural tests mutate sequences and relax their structures. Cα-RMSD, Rosetta repulsive energy, and TM-score assess whether structure remains similar. (PDF p. 4).
