papers.title: Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (Unless SETH is False)
indicators: The authors seek evidence that the known near-quadratic bounds for exact edit distance are tight. (PDF p. 1).
Edit distance adds costs across aligned gadgets. Thus, every nonorthogonal vector pair must have the same gadget cost, independent of the number of shared 1s. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: On the Complexity of Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: Jain and colleagues study sequence-to-graph alignment under Hamming and edit distance. They distinguish changes to the query, graph labels, or both. (PDF p. 1).

Table 1 compares asymptotic running times with prior algorithms for edit distance, arbitrary linear costs, and affine gaps. The new bound matches the listed best edit-distance bound and improves the listed bounds for the other two settings. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast Gap-Affine Pairwise Alignment Using the Wavefront Algorithm
indicators: The abstract states O(ns) time and O(s^2) memory, where n is sequence length and s is alignment score. (PDF p. 2).
The authors argue that conventional matrix methods perform similar work for identical and divergent sequences. WFA makes work depend on alignment score. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improved Tools for Biological Sequence Comparison
indicators: FASTA uses a lookup table to find runs of ktup identities. It selects ten diagonal regions, rescores them with a substitution matrix, and retains their highest scoring subregions. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Bounded Weighted Edit Distance
indicators: The authors give a dynamic algorithm for bounded weighted edit distance with arbitrary normalized edit costs. A fixed threshold k controls preprocessing and update costs. (PDF p. 1).
Determine how quickly weighted edit distance can be maintained when strings change and the distance is small. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein structure alignment by Reseek improves sensitivity to remote homologs
indicators: Alignment quality, AQ, combines LDDT-mu, alignment score, a reversed-query alignment score and length terms. Parameters use SCOP40 training with hold-out validation. An empirical distribution converts AQ to E-values. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Algorithms for Jumbled Indexing, Jumbled Border and Jumbled Square on run-length encoded strings
indicators: Build an index that returns all substrings whose histograms equal a query histogram. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Progressive Sequence Alignment as a Prerequisite to Correct Phylogenetic Trees
indicators: Construct reliable multiple sequence alignments to infer correct phylogenetic trees. (PDF p. 1).
Multiple sequence alignment of globin and kinase protein families. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Next-Generation Sequence Assembly: Four Stages of Data Processing and Computational Challenges
indicators: Multiple sequence alignment filters align candidate erroneous reads with trusted reads to infer consensus bases. Coral and ECHO implement this approach. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: A Survey on Sequence Alignment Algorithms and State-of-the-Art Aligners
indicators: The authors organize pairwise and multiple sequence aligners by common algorithmic stages. Their literature collection contains 158 documents. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: BetaAlign: a deep learning approach for multiple sequence alignment
indicators: BetaAlign trains transformers to convert unaligned sequences into multiple sequence alignments using simulated training examples. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: CLUSTAL W: Improving the Sensitivity of Progressive Multiple Sequence Alignment Through Sequence Weighting, Position-Specific Gap Penalties and Weight Matrix Choice
indicators: Progressive alignment does not guarantee a globally optimal multiple alignment. Reliability decreases when all sequence pairs have less than approximately 25–30% identity. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: MAFFT: A Novel Method for Rapid Multiple Sequence Alignment Based on Fast Fourier Transform
indicators: Reduce multiple alignment time through rapid detection of homologous segments. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Recent Evolutions of Multiple Sequence Alignment Algorithms
indicators: The author reviews developments in multiple sequence alignment algorithms, focusing on consistency and template methods. (PDF p. 1).
Review modern multiple sequence alignment strategies that move beyond pure sequence-based progressive alignment. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: MUSCLE: a multiple sequence alignment method with reduced time and space complexity
indicators: PSI-BLAST sequence selection and alignment errors can bias the profile-function test. Results may not transfer directly to profiles built iteratively during multiple alignment. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: An nf-core framework for the systematic comparison of alternative modeling tools: the multiple sequence alignment case study
indicators: The authors present nf-core/multiplesequencealign for deploying and comparing protein multiple sequence alignment methods. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Multiple sequence alignment with the Clustal series of programs
indicators: Clustal builds a multiple alignment through successive pairwise alignments in guide-tree order. The original implementation combined progressive alignment with memory-efficient dynamic programming. (PDF p. 1).
The timing comparison measures neighbour-joining without distance-matrix calculation and also measures complete multiple alignment. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Measuring the distance between multiple sequence alignments
indicators: Blackburne and Whelan introduce four metrics for comparing multiple sequence alignments. The metrics use different amounts of gap information. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Optimizing multiple sequence alignments using a genetic algorithm based on three objectives: structural information, non-gaps percentage and totally conserved columns
indicators: MO-SAStrE refines protein multiple sequence alignments with NSGA-II. It jointly maximizes STRIKE score, non-gap percentage and totally conserved column percentage. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Optimal alignment between groups of sequences and its application to multiple sequence alignment
indicators: The algorithms support progressive alignment and randomized group realignment for multiple sequence alignment. (PDF p. 6).
The methods align protein families through a given binary tree or refine an existing multiple alignment through randomized grouping. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: End-to-end learning of multiple sequence alignments
indicators: The Learned Alignment Module constructs differentiable multiple sequence alignments with smooth Smith–Waterman. A downstream learning objective can update the alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning (Alphafold)
indicators: AlphaFold predicts residue distance distributions from sequence and multiple sequence alignment features. These distributions define a protein-specific structural potential. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Characterization of pairwise and multiple sequence alignment errors
indicators: The authors compare simulated true alignments with ALIGN pairwise alignments and ClustalW multiple sequence alignments. (PDF p. 2).
Identify the sources and characteristics of multiple sequence alignment errors. Measure reconstruction error against simulated true alignments. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Sequential and Parallel Algorithms for the All-Substrings Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present sequential and parallel algorithms for the all-substrings longest common subsequence problem. (PDF p. 2).
The algorithm computes LCS lengths for all substrings of one string against another using Monge matrix properties. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Coarse-Grained Parallel Algorithm for the All-Substrings Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present a BSP/CGM parallel algorithm for all-substrings longest common subsequence (ALCS). It computes LCS lengths for A and every substring of B. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: T-Coffee: A Novel Method for Fast and Accurate Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: The authors introduce T-Coffee for progressive multiple sequence alignment with reduced greedy error accumulation. (PDF p. 1).
Multiple alignment of divergent protein and nucleotide sequences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: CREMSA: compressed indexing of (ultra) large multiple sequence alignments
indicators: CREMSA compresses multiple sequence alignments by column runs and supports queries without full decompression. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Gap Costs for Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: The cost definitions apply to optimal multiple alignment of biological sequences, including tree and star alignments. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: A flexible multiple sequence alignment program
indicators: GENALIGN constructs multiple sequence alignments through clustered pairwise alignments. (PDF p. 2).
The author states that the significance of a multiple sequence alignment is generally difficult to evaluate. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: Gapped BLAST and PSI-BLAST: A New Generation of Protein Database Search Programs
indicators: PSI-BLAST forms a multiple alignment from BLAST results, converts it to a position-specific score matrix, and searches the database with that matrix. (PDF p. 13).
Inaccurate or unrelated pairwise alignments can affect the evolving multiple alignment. The authors propose additional realignment as a future improvement. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: Fast and sensitive multiple sequence alignments on a microcomputer
indicators: Interpretation: optimality of each two-group alignment does not establish optimality of the complete multiple alignment. The method follows a fixed dendrogram and preserves earlier gaps. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Improvement in accuracy of multiple sequence alignment using novel group-to-group sequence alignment algorithm with piecewise linear gap cost
indicators: PRIME uses group-to-group alignment with a piecewise linear gap cost to improve multiple sequence alignment. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: The CLUSTAL_X windows interface: flexible strategies for multiple sequence alignment aided by quality analysis tools
indicators: The authors introduce CLUSTAL_X, a graphical user interface for the ClustalW multiple sequence alignment engine. (PDF p. 1).
Facilitate interactive quality assessment and local realignment of multiple sequence alignments in a windowed environment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Profile Hidden Markov Models
indicators: Profile HMMs convert multiple sequence alignments into probabilistic scoring models for remote homology searches. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: M2Align: parallel multiple sequence alignment with a multi-objective metaheuristic
indicators: The authors aim to reduce the cost of multi-objective multiple sequence alignment through multicore execution. (PDF p. 2).
The authors argue that multiple alignment scores capture different properties. A multi-objective search can return alternative trade-off solutions in one run. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: ProbCons: Probabilistic Consistency-Based Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: ProbCons constructs progressive protein multiple sequence alignments with pair-HMM posterior probabilities and probabilistic consistency. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Mugsy: fast multiple alignment of closely related whole genomes
indicators: The method combines Nucmer pairwise alignments, an alignment graph, locally collinear block identification, and SeqAn::T-Coffee multiple alignment. (PDF p. 2).

Nucmer searches all genome pairs. Delta-filter retains matches in the highest-scoring chains of both sequences for multiple alignment. Scores combine match length with squared sequence identity. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Muscle5: High-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased assessments of sequence homology and phylogeny
indicators: Muscle5 generates ensembles of accurate multiple sequence alignments by changing HMM parameters and guide-tree joining order. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: COFFEE: an objective function for multiple sequence alignments
indicators: COFFEE scores a multiple sequence alignment by its consistency with a library of pairwise alignments. (PDF p. 3).
The authors aim to improve multiple alignment accuracy through consistency with pairwise reference alignments. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Protein 3D Structure Computed from Evolutionary Sequence Variation
indicators: EVfold infers residue couplings from multiple sequence alignments with a maximum entropy model. It converts these couplings into distance constraints for protein structure generation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein embedding based alignment
indicators: The authors propose extending the scoring function to multiple sequence alignment. They did not establish its accuracy for that task. (PDF p. 13).
The benchmark contained more than 12,000 pairwise alignments extracted from BAliBASE multiple sequence alignments across five references. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: TM-align: A Protein Structure Alignment Algorithm Based on the TM-score
indicators: Initial fragment alignments are generated using gapless eight-residue superposition and secondary structures. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BIMSA: accelerating long sequence alignment using processing-in-memory
indicators: BIMSA replaces recursion with iterative breakpoint subdivision. It applies regular WFA when a subproblem's score permits its memory use to fit the allocated WRAM. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Parallel Algorithm for Longest Common Subsequence in a String
indicators: The authors argue that dynamic programming avoids repeated subproblem calculations that make brute-force subsequence enumeration expensive. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm distributes matrix work across processors through OpenMP. The authors describe the partition as block-stripped. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BAli-Phy version 3: model-based co-estimation of alignment and phylogeny
indicators: Users can analyze multiple partitions and independently fix or estimate each partition's alignment. (PDF p. 2).
Runtime remains O(L²) in sequence length L for each partition. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast text searching: allowing errors
indicators: Partition filtering produces fewer accidental exact matches with a large alphabet. Small alphabets increase such matches and reduce its effectiveness. (PDF p. 7).
A partition-based filtering search accelerates approximate matching by using exact matches. Its performance depends on alphabet size. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Protein Structure Comparison by Alignment of Distance Matrices
indicators: Hexapeptide fragment pairs with similar distance patterns are assembled using Monte Carlo search. (PDF p. 5).
Hexapeptides are decomposed into overlapping tetrapeptides to refine fragment boundaries. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: MSAProbs: multiple sequence alignment based on pair hidden Markov models and partition function posterior probabilities
indicators: MSAProbs combines pair-HMM and partition-function posterior probabilities for multiple protein sequence alignment. (PDF p. 1).

The authors motivate the combined probability model with earlier results on long terminal extensions. They suggest that partition-function probabilities can help locate highly similar regions. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: An Improved Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm for Reducing Memory Complexity in Global Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: The reported comparison considers memory use against full-table LCS and qualitative runtime and memory differences against divide and conquer. (PDF p. 5).
The authors state that SB_LCS is faster than divide and conquer, but uses more memory. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: On Multiple Insertion-Deletion Correcting Codes
indicators: Partition binary words by the residue of their weighted moment: sum(v_i x_i) ≡ a mod u. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning (Alphafold)
indicators: The data split contains 29,427 training domains and 1,820 test domains. Homologous superfamilies stay within one partition. A 377-domain subset supplies the reported internal tests. (PDF p. 6).
CASP13 results include fragment assembly and gradient descent systems. The submission procedure changed during the assessment. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Fast discrete convolution in R2 with radial kernels using non-uniform fast Fourier transform with nonequispaced frequencies
indicators: Efficient Bessel Decomposition (EBD) reduces the number of frequency samples. The authors report faster convolution evaluation after longer precomputation. (PDF p. 3).
The author aims to extend Sparse Cardinal Sine Decomposition from three dimensions to two dimensions using Bessel functions. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Efficient algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem with sequential substring constraints
indicators: The objective is to combine sequence-inclusion and string-inclusion constraints in one problem. Single-character partitions and a single string partition recover the earlier inclusion variants. (PDF p. 2).
For overlapping constraints, each DP cell examines O(l_k) overlap choices for partition k. Summing partition lengths gives O(mnr) DP time. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Computing the longest topological common subsequence of a symbol-wise totally ordered directed acyclic graph and a sequence
indicators: An independent set contains at most one pair from each exclusive list. A partition into L such lists therefore gives an upper bound of L on subsequence length. (PDF p. 3).
Process prefixes of B in increasing order. Maintain a partition of matching pairs into exclusive lists and an independent set that selects one pair from each list. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Different Longest Common Subsequence Algorithms
indicators: The comparison covers dynamic programming, divide and conquer, match-point processing, and diagonal edit-graph traversal. (PDF p. 3).
The authors motivate dynamic programming through optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Stored subproblem results support later computations. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: On the Economical Construction of the Transitive Closure of a Directed Graph
indicators: The algorithm combines a partition into ranks with precomputed unions for products of multivalued mappings. (PDF p. 2).
Partition B into blocks of at most ln q elements. For each block, enumerate all subsets and construct their images under β. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming on DAGs with Small Width
indicators: The authors formulate sparse dynamic programming and co-linear chaining on directed acyclic graphs parameterized by path width. (PDF p. 1).
Align sequences and co-linear fragment chains to pangenome DAGs efficiently when path width k is small. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming I: Linear Cost Functions
indicators: The authors introduce sparse dynamic programming algorithms for sequence alignment and RNA structure with linear gap costs. (PDF p. 1).
The method computes recurrences over M sparse fragment points in O(n + M log log min(M, n^2/M)) time. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Fast and Practical Bit-Vector Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors propose Hirschberg divide-and-conquer to recover an actual LCS. Bit-vector length computation locates recursive middle points. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Fast and sensitive multiple sequence alignments on a microcomputer
indicators: Myers-Miller alignment recursively finds optimal alignment midpoints. This divide-and-conquer procedure uses memory proportional to sequence length. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Optimal Alignments in Linear Space
indicators: Myers and Miller adapt Hirschberg's divide-and-conquer method to Gotoh's algorithm for affine gap costs. (PDF p. 1).
Recursive subproblem areas decrease geometrically. The analysis gives a leading time cost below twice the top-level matrix computation. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming II: Convex and Concave Cost Functions
indicators: The authors extend sparse dynamic programming to non-linear, convex, and concave gap cost functions. (PDF p. 1).
Generalize sparse dynamic programming to non-linear cost functions without incurring full quadratic overhead. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming for Longest Common Subsequence from Fragments
indicators: The authors present sparse dynamic programming algorithms for computing the LCS from fragment matches. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm runs in O(M log M) time and O(M) space, where M is the number of fragment pairs. (PDF p. 23).

papers.title: A draft human pangenome reference
indicators: PGGB uses all-to-all assembly alignment. It is reference-free except that GRCh38 and T2T-CHM13 help partition contigs by chromosome. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: WFA-GPU: gap-affine pairwise read-alignment using GPUs
indicators: Bit-parallel 32-bit operations compare 16-nucleotide blocks simultaneously to minimize thread divergence. (PDF p. 6).
WFA-GPU achieves 2.7x to 4.8x overall speedup on PacBio and Nanopore reads compared to optimized CPU implementations. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: TM-align: A Protein Structure Alignment Algorithm Based on the TM-score
indicators: The authors present TM-align, a protein structure alignment algorithm that optimizes TM-score rather than RMSD. (PDF p. 1).
Dynamic programming iteratively refines residue pairings guided by rotation matrices that optimize the TM-score. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Rapid and Sensitive Protein Similarity Searches
indicators: High-scoring diagonal regions are identified and joined, followed by local dynamic programming optimization. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A trimodal protein language model enables advanced protein searches
indicators: The model supports nine retrieval directions within and between its three modalities. Inference uses maximum inner product search. (PDF p. 3).
The authors retrieve enzyme descriptions from a curated EC text database and apply a maximum-separation rule for annotation. (PDF p. 15).

papers.title: Computing a Longest Common Subsequence for Multiple Sequences
indicators: MRepeDPH adds a pheromone matrix inspired by ant colony optimization. It updates this matrix with the LCS weight matrix and uses both to derive sequence weights. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: The String-to-String Correction Problem
indicators: Edit distance is defined as the minimum-cost sequence of character insertions, deletions, and substitutions. (PDF p. 1).
Compute the minimum-cost edit script transforming string A of length m into string B of length n. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Next-Generation Sequence Assembly: Four Stages of Data Processing and Computational Challenges
indicators: Assembly quality depends on the dataset, assembly algorithm, k-mer size, and minimum overlap length. The authors describe a tradeoff between contiguity and accuracy. (PDF p. 14).
PBcR aligns short reads to long PacBio reads and seeks a maximum matching to construct a consensus sequence. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: BIMSA: accelerating long sequence alignment using processing-in-memory
indicators: It supports optimal alignment of sequences up to 100,000 bases. (PDF p. 1).
They characterize memory bottlenecks, optimize BiWFA for UPMEM, and compare it with CPU and PIM implementations. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Survey on Sequence Alignment Algorithms and State-of-the-Art Aligners
indicators: The review contrasts optimal dynamic programming with faster word-based heuristics. Seed-and-extend methods restrict the regions that require expensive alignment computation. (PDF p. 9).
The genetic algorithm framework creates an alignment population, evaluates an objective function, selects fitter alignments, and applies crossover and mutation. (PDF p. 18).

papers.title: Sketching, Streaming, and Fine-Grained Complexity of (Weighted) LCS
indicators: String gadgets over fixed alphabets encode vector orthogonality into optimal weighted alignment scores. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: Optimal Gap-Affine Alignment in O(s) Space
indicators: The authors present bidirectional wavefront alignment (BiWFA). It computes optimal gap-affine alignments in O(ns) time and O(s) memory, excluding input storage. Here, n is sequence length and s is the optimal alignment score. (PDF p. 2).
BiWFA computes forward and reverse wavefronts. It finds a breakpoint near half the optimal score and recursively aligns the two remaining parts. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: CLUSTAL W: Improving the Sensitivity of Progressive Multiple Sequence Alignment Through Sequence Weighting, Position-Specific Gap Penalties and Weight Matrix Choice
indicators: Address alignment parameter choice through adaptive matrices and gap penalties. The authors do not directly solve the local minimum problem. (PDF p. 2).
The authors propose future refinement through iterative or stochastic optimization from several starting parameter sets. This requires a suitable objective function. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Protein Structure Comparison by Alignment of Distance Matrices
indicators: The method identifies contact patterns and aligns them using Monte Carlo optimization. (PDF p. 1).
The Monte Carlo optimization is heuristic and may fail to identify the globally optimal alignment. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: MSAProbs: multiple sequence alignment based on pair hidden Markov models and partition function posterior probabilities
indicators: Weighting gave small, dataset-dependent gains. The default combination favored PREFAB accuracy while retaining BAliBASE accuracy, but did not maximize BAliBASE SPS. (PDF p. 6).
Pairwise global alignment uses posterior probabilities as scores and zero gap penalties. Distance equals one minus the optimal score divided by the shorter sequence length. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Identification of Direct Residue Contacts in Protein–Protein Interaction by Message Passing
indicators: The authors use a maximum-entropy model to match single-position and pair frequencies while avoiding unnecessary constraints. (PDF p. 3).

A pairwise maximum-entropy model represents direct couplings and local amino acid preferences. Marginal estimation and coupling updates repeat until model frequencies meet the specified precision. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Analysis of Evolutionary Algorithms for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: They prove exponential lower bounds on expected optimization time. The bounds apply even to instances with two binary sequences. (PDF p. 16).

Theorem 7 bounds the probability of finding an optimum within t fitness evaluations by t·exp(−Ω(n)). It covers all crossover probabilities and polynomial parent and offspring population sizes. (PDF p. 15).

papers.title: Maximal common subsequence algorithms
indicators: The author argues that removing the maximum-length requirement permits faster construction than the corresponding longest-common-subsequence problems. (PDF p. 2).
The construction does not optimize subsequence length. It seeks an arbitrary maximal common subsequence. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Multiple sequence alignment with the Clustal series of programs
indicators: The authors state that users need access to alignment parameters because defaults are not optimal for every problem. (PDF p. 2).
The Gonnet series became the default residue comparison matrices for protein alignment after parameter optimization. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Matching for Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: The block matrix stores the optimum LCS value between prefixes ending at run boundaries. X has l runs and Y has k runs. (PDF p. 3).
Tree queries find the best forced-path scores for the relevant row and column. The block value is the maximum of these scores and the two adjacent prefix values. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: Levenshtein Distance, Sequence Comparison and Biological Database Search
indicators: The authors describe a duality between minimum-distance and maximum-similarity alignment. Appropriate score weights give the same optimal alignments. (PDF p. 3).
Levenshtein distance counts the minimum substitutions, single-letter insertions, and single-letter deletions needed to transform one string into another. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A fast homology program for aligning biological sequences
indicators: Taylor presents procedures that compute evolutionary distance and an optimal alignment path in one pass of MN iterations. (PDF p. 1).
Another version uses a word array to store path segments. A 16-bit layout permits gaps of up to 127 elements in either sequence and supports enumeration of all optimal paths. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: An Improved Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm for Reducing Memory Complexity in Global Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: The authors aim to reduce forward-pass storage while retaining enough information to construct an optimal LCS. (PDF p. 1).
The authors state that the optimal traceback stays within the four bounds. Values outside the required region need not be stacked. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Algorithms for Computing the Longest Parameterized Common Subsequence
indicators: Find the maximum common subsequence length under bounds on successive index distances and on the difference between these distances in the two strings. (PDF p. 3).
The max-queue uses a window of K2 − K1 + 1. Dummy insertions remove expired entries before a maximum query. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: On the Theory and Computation of Evolutionary Distances
indicators: Sellers defines evolutionary distance as the minimum total weight of mutations and deletions that make two sequences alike. (PDF p. 2).
The formal construction starts with a metric on symbols, including the neutral element. Evolutionary distance is the minimum over equivalent sequence representations. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Accelign: a GPU-based library for accelerating pairwise sequence alignment
indicators: The high-level API selects a configuration from the maximum query length in a batch. Queries up to 512 use one tile; longer queries use multiple tiles of up to 1024. (PDF p. 18).

papers.title: A General Method Applicable to the Search for Similarities in the Amino Acid Sequence of Two Proteins
indicators: The authors present a computer method to find a maximum match between two protein sequences. It permits gaps and preserves sequence order. (PDF p. 1).
The method aims to exclude comparisons that cannot contribute to the maximum match. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Optimal alignment between groups of sequences and its application to multiple sequence alignment
indicators: Algorithm D exactly optimizes the group-to-group sum-of-pairs score with affine gap costs. Its typical computation cost is close to O(MNL^2). (PDF p. 1).
Obtain exact group-to-group score optimization at a practical computation cost. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Efficient seeding for error-prone sequences with SubseqHash2
indicators: The dynamic program first solves subproblems by recurrence. It then finds the minimum-ranked subsequence for each order and window, reusing subproblems across windows. (PDF p. 4).
The implementation can generate only the requested t seeds during optimization. Larger k reduces sensitivity and false positives for fixed n. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: End-to-end learning of multiple sequence alignments
indicators: SMURF first uses BasicAlign to minimize squared differences from an averaged MSA. TrainMRF then uses masked language modeling to update both MRF parameters and alignment convolutions. (PDF p. 3).
LAM can replace the AlphaFold input alignment and receive gradients that maximize predicted structure confidence. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: On Multiple Insertion-Deletion Correcting Codes
indicators: The authors state that any s-insertion/deletion correcting code has minimum Hamming distance at least s + 1. (PDF p. 2).
The minimum Hamming distance gives the correction-capability upper bound s ≤ d_min − 1. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Multiple protein structure alignment at scale with FoldMason
indicators: FoldMason encodes structures as 3Di+AA strings and computes ungapped alignments for all pairs. It sorts pair scores to construct a minimum spanning guide tree. (PDF p. 2).
The refinement benchmark used 1,000 iterations and fixed random seed 48335597. Separate runs optimized LDDT with and without gappy columns. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning (Alphafold)
indicators: The described system optimizes backbone torsion angles with L-BFGS and repeated initializations to generate structures. (PDF p. 3).
Optimize whole protein chains without first assigning domain boundaries. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Characterization of pairwise and multiple sequence alignment errors
indicators: The authors argue that an optimal alignment score does not guarantee historical accuracy. True segments can have lower scores than incorrect segments or share the same optimal score. (PDF p. 2).
The authors link the bias toward shorter alignments to score optimization. With the same number of matches, shorter alignments usually receive higher scores. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast and exact gap-affine partial order alignment
indicators: POASTA computes optimal sequence-to-graph alignments with gap-affine penalties. It uses A* search, greedy exact matching, and topology-based pruning. (PDF p. 2).
The authors aim to reduce runtime and memory use while preserving optimal sequence-to-graph alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Bit-parallel sequence-to-graph alignment
indicators: Find a graph path with minimum edit distance to the complete query. Mismatches, insertions, and deletions have unit cost. (PDF p. 2).
The merge algorithm calculates score differences in parallel chunks. It builds comparison masks and a picking mask to form the elementwise minimum of two encoded columns. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Algorithms for approximate string matching
indicators: The objective is to compute edit distance and an optimal editing sequence more efficiently than the basic O(mn) table method. (PDF p. 3).
The basic recurrence computes prefix edit distances from deletion, insertion, and substitution costs. A backward minimizing path recovers an optimal editing sequence. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: MacCorles: Minimum Alignment Cost Computation on Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: Their run-length encoded algorithm outputs an optimum alignment in O(mN + nM) time and O(nm) working space. N and M are decoded lengths. n and m are run counts. (PDF p. 16).
Select the shortest alignment among alignments with the maximum number of equal pairs. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Construction of Phylogenetic Trees Walter
indicators: The method computes minimum mutation distances between homologous proteins and estimates ancestral branch lengths. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm computes a minimum mutation distance matrix between pairs of homologous sequences. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Geometric algebra generation of molecular surfaces
indicators: Piecewise initial data assign zero inside atomic spheres and one outside. Gaussian initial data use the maximum of atom-centered Gaussian functions, with a scale parameter of 3 Å. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Fast discrete convolution in R2 with radial kernels using non-uniform fast Fourier transform with nonequispaced frequencies
indicators: The circular-quadrature error allocation bounds the maximum error of the trigonometric kernel representation by epsilon. (PDF p. 19).
EBD approximates the radial kernel on an annulus with a constant and a sum of zero-order Bessel functions. Coefficients minimize a radius-weighted squared derivative error. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Faster Algorithm Computing String Edit Distances
indicators: Masek and Paterson present an algorithm for minimum-cost string editing with insertion, deletion, and replacement of individual symbols. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm can produce an optimal edit sequence. Longest common subsequence computation is a special case. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: QuickEd: high-performance exact sequence alignment based on bound-and-align
indicators: QuickEd first estimates an upper bound on edit distance. It then uses that bound to restrict DP computation and recover an optimal alignment. (PDF p. 2).
The authors state O(n) time and O(1) memory for score approximation, and O(n ŝ) time for exact alignment. Here, ŝ is an upper bound on the optimal score. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Different Longest Common Subsequence Algorithms
indicators: The authors motivate dynamic programming through optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Stored subproblem results support later computations. (PDF p. 1).
Hirschberg combines forward and reverse dynamic-programming rows to locate a midpoint on an optimal path. Divide and conquer then supports sequence reconstruction with linear space. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Direct-Coupling Analysis of Residue Coevolution Captures Native Contacts Across Many Protein Families
indicators: A pairwise maximum-entropy model matches single-column and paired-column frequencies. The mean-field approximation estimates couplings as the negative inverse connected-correlation matrix. (PDF p. 7).
Evaluation excludes nearby sequence positions and defines contacts by minimum atomic distance below 8 Å. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Building pangenome graphs
indicators: WFMASH uses BiWFλ to compare 256-bp segments through a callback. It assembles the final base-level alignment from alignments of segment pairs on the optimal path. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: An O(ND) Difference Algorithm and Its Variations
indicators: The algorithm takes O(ND) time, where N is total input length and D is minimum edit-script length. It is intended for inputs with few differences. (PDF p. 1).
The greedy search retains the current furthest-reaching endpoints in vector V. These endpoints suffice to report the optimal length. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: An Evolutionary Model for Maximum Likelihood Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: The authors derive maximum likelihood alignment of two DNA sequences from a statistical model with explicit transition probabilities. (PDF p. 1).
The likelihood surface for a selected best alignment is not differentiable everywhere. The authors describe the summed likelihood surface as differentiable and easier to optimize. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Gap Costs for Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: The objective is to extend useful pairwise gap costs to multiple alignments while keeping optimal alignment computationally practical. (PDF p. 2).
Gap and substitution costs jointly determine the optimal alignment. The author therefore argues that they must have a common rationale. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Linear Space Algorithm for Computing Maximal Common Subsequences
indicators: The split theorem states that maximizing the sum of prefix and suffix subsequence lengths over split positions in B gives the full optimum. (PDF p. 2).
The algorithm constructs a common subsequence of maximum length for two strings. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and accurate multiple-protein-sequence alignment at scale with FAMSA2
indicators: Medoid guide tree construction takes O(M N log N) time. N is the sequence count, and M is the maximum subtree size. The authors report accuracy comparable to quadratic-time single-linkage trees. (PDF p. 2).
Single-linkage guide tree construction uses Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm in linear space. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Sparse Dynamic Programming on DAGs with Small Width
indicators: The algorithm runs in O(k |V| + N log N) time on DAGs decomposed into k minimum path covers. (PDF p. 3).
Complexity is analyzed in terms of the minimum path cover k of the graph using Dilworth theorem. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein Homology Detection by HMM–HMM Comparison
indicators: HHsearch uses Viterbi dynamic programming to find the HMM alignment path with the maximum log-sum-of-odds score. (PDF p. 3).
The correlation weight of 0.1 was selected on 317-by-317 pairwise alignments. The secondary structure weight had a broad empirical optimum near 0.15. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Parasail: SIMD C Library for Global, Semi-Global, and Local Pairwise Sequence Alignments
indicators: The author aims to provide fast optimal pairwise alignment routines that other software packages can integrate. (PDF p. 9).
Dynamic programming provides an optimal alignment for a specified scoring function. The author contrasts this guarantee with heuristics that can return suboptimal alignments. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Chirality in a quaternionic representation of the genetic code
indicators: The authors fit three small protein structures with particle swarm optimization and report alpha-carbon RMSDs below 0.17 Å. (PDF p. 13).

Particle swarm optimization fits the unknown real order quaternions. The fitness measure is alpha-carbon RMSD against reference coordinates, calculated with an implementation of the Kabsch algorithm. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: A flexible multiple sequence alignment program
indicators: The author argues that limiting the region set is useful because selection of an optimal region sequence has quadratic cost in the number of regions. (PDF p. 3).
Region generation takes L log L time, where L is the sum of sequence lengths. Optimal region-path selection has cost proportional to the square of the region count. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (Unless SETH is False)
indicators: The analysis expresses edit distance as the minimum total cost of deletions and substitutions that transform both strings into a common string. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: On the Complexity of Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: A graph-label change affects every visit to that vertex on a cyclic alignment path. A query change affects only one query position. Thus, permitted edit locations can change the optimal score. (PDF p. 3).
The correctness proof shows that the two queues produce vertices in minimum-distance order. This reproduces the choices of Dijkstra’s algorithm. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: Compute optimal ungapped scores for 32 targets in parallel with AVX2. Pass alignments above 15 bits to vectorized Smith–Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: HPRC2: A human pangenome reference with near-complete coverage of common genetic variation
indicators: The tree coordinate strategy constructs a minimum spanning tree over the graph. It indexes edges to describe off-reference variants in formats such as VCF. (PDF p. 15).
The authors report that optimized sample selection covers over 99% of common variants observed in the All of Us v8 cohort. (PDF p. 35).

papers.title: Theseus: fast and optimal affine-gap sequence-tograph alignment
indicators: Compute exact optimal affine-gap alignments of sequences to pangenome graphs in sub-quadratic time. (PDF p. 2).
A memory-efficient backtrace algorithm recovers optimal alignment paths directly from wavefront checkpoints. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Fast and Practical Bit-Vector Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: With unit insertion and deletion costs and substitution cost two, LCS length p and optimal edit cost d satisfy p = (n + m − d)/2. (PDF p. 2).
The authors reduce the stated bit-wise operation count from five in the optimized Allison–Dix expression to four. Their expression uses addition instead of subtraction. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: MAFFT version 5: improvement in accuracy of multiple sequence alignment
indicators: G-INS-i uses global pairwise alignments with an FFT approximation. H-INS-i uses FASTA with Smith–Waterman optimization. F-INS-i uses FASTA without that optimization. (PDF p. 3).
Dynamic programming aligns groups using substitution scores and importance values. Iterative refinement then optimizes the WSP+I objective. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Gapped BLAST and PSI-BLAST: A New Generation of Protein Database Search Programs
indicators: Gapped extension uses dynamic programming in both directions from a seed. It retains cells whose optimal local score is no more than Xg below the best score found. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Exact global alignment using A* with chaining seed heuristic and match pruning
indicators: Gap-chaining uses the maximum of seed cost and gap cost. Adding these costs could count an indel twice and break admissibility. (PDF p. 5).
An optimal alignment is a shortest path in a graph with zero-cost matches and unit-cost substitutions, insertions, and deletions. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Solving longest common subsequence problems via a transformation to the maximum clique problem
indicators: The authors transform constrained LCS problems into instances of the maximum clique problem. (PDF p. 2).
Exact and heuristic maximum clique solvers are applied to solve repetition-free and arc-preserving LCS variants. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and sensitive multiple sequence alignments on a microcomputer
indicators: The earlier approximate progressive method worked well mainly for closely related sequences. Linear-space optimal pairwise alignment made a more sensitive approach practical within limited memory. (PDF p. 1).
Myers-Miller alignment recursively finds optimal alignment midpoints. This divide-and-conquer procedure uses memory proportional to sequence length. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast Optimal Alignment
indicators: Fickett changes the computation order of an alignment matrix to find an optimal alignment after evaluating only part of the matrix. (PDF p. 1).
Reduce the cost of Needleman–Wunsch-type alignment while retaining an optimal result. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improvement in accuracy of multiple sequence alignment using novel group-to-group sequence alignment algorithm with piecewise linear gap cost
indicators: Exact group-to-group optimization requires alternative partial paths. Their number can grow exponentially, which motivates omission of the candidate list. (PDF p. 3).
PRIME optimizes a weighted sum-of-pairs objective with a simpler dynamic programming method. It omits candidate lists and anchoring heuristics. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Fast Gap-Affine Pairwise Alignment Using the Wavefront Algorithm
indicators: WFA-Adapt prunes distant outer diagonals to reduce work and memory. This heuristic can miss the optimal alignment. (PDF p. 5).
Wavefronts store offsets of furthest-reaching points on diagonals. The first wavefront to reach the matrix endpoint gives the optimal alignment. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improved Tools for Biological Sequence Comparison
indicators: FASTA can produce an initial score above its final optimized score. The initial calculation joins regions, but the final alignment uses a restricted band. (PDF p. 2).
RDF2 calculates single-region, joined-region, and optimized scores for shuffled sequences. Users can select global shuffling or shuffling within short blocks. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Relative Position based Algorithm to find out the Longest Common Subsequence from Multiple Biological Sequences
indicators: It selects the character with minimum Z. The stated tie rule uses minimum X when the two lowest Z values are equal. (PDF p. 3).
Pruning rule 2 first computes Z for the candidate with minimum X. It then removes candidates whose X is at least that Z value. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Faster algorithms for RNA-folding using the Four-Russians method
indicators: Improve serial and parallel runtime for the maximum non-crossing base-pair problem. (PDF p. 1).
Preprocessing enumerates horizontal and vertical difference-vector pairs. It stores the maximum cumulative-sum combination and its index for traceback. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Algorithms for Two Versions of LCS Problem for Indeterminate Strings
indicators: Develop ILCS and CILCS algorithms whose bounds account for alphabet size, maximum set size ℓ, and match counts. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An Improved Algorithm for Matching Biological Sequences
indicators: Each matrix cell requires a minimum over three candidates for D and a minimum over two candidates for each gap state. This gives MN constant-cost updates. (PDF p. 2).
D(m,n) is the minimum of the diagonal score plus the residue-pair cost and the two gap-state scores P(m,n) and Q(m,n). (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Alignment of Whole Genomes
indicators: The system aligns small polymorphic gaps with dynamic programming equivalent to Smith–Waterman. This gives an optimal local alignment under specified insertion and mutation costs. (PDF p. 5).
For large polymorphic regions, the authors propose recursive matching with a lower minimum MUM length. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
indicators: LoL-align iteratively optimizes a local log-odds score for protein structure alignment. The score uses intramolecular Cα distances and sequence distances. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Matching Sequences under Deletion/Insertion Constraints
indicators: The unconstrained algorithm stores prefix maxima in W. Each cell takes the maximum of the upper cell, the left cell, and the diagonal cell plus an equality indicator. (PDF p. 1).
For positive q, V_q selects between a diagonal predecessor in V_q and a prefix maximum in W_(q−1), then adds the equality indicator. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: M2Align: parallel multiple sequence alignment with a multi-objective metaheuristic
indicators: M2Align reimplements MO-SAStrE in Java using NSGA-II. It optimizes STRIKE, totally conserved columns, and non-gap percentage together. (PDF p. 3).
The authors aim to reduce the cost of multi-objective multiple sequence alignment through multicore execution. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Heaviest Increasing-Common Subsequence Problems
indicators: Find increasing and common subsequences with maximum total weight. Weights can depend on symbols and their positions. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Optimal Alignments in Linear Space
indicators: The method produces one optimal alignment in linear space while retaining O(MN) time. (PDF p. 1).
The authors provide a portable C implementation that returns the minimum cost and an optimal sequence of editing operations. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Finding the longest common subsequence for multiple biological sequences by ant colony optimization
indicators: The authors propose ant colony optimization (ACO) to find approximate longest common subsequences for multiple biological sequences. (PDF p. 1).
The authors compare solution lengths through percentage gains relative to ExpA and BNMAS. These gains compare algorithms rather than establish distance from an optimum. (PDF p. 15).

papers.title: A Differentiable Alignment Framework for Sequence-to-Sequence Modeling via Optimal Transport
indicators: The authors introduce Sequence Optimal Transport Distance (SOTD), a sequence pseudo-metric based on differentiable one-dimensional optimal transport. (PDF p. 1).
They derive Optimal Temporal Transport Classification (OTTC) loss to learn an alignment and speech recognition jointly. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: ProbCons: Probabilistic Consistency-Based Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: They identify maximum expected accuracy and probabilistic consistency as the main sources of accuracy improvement. (PDF p. 7).
Progressive alignment does not guarantee an optimum for the probabilistic consistency objective. Iterative refinement is a heuristic improvement step. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: Mugsy: fast multiple alignment of closely related whole genomes
indicators: An anchor graph identifies collinear paths and merges regions after short-block filtering. Maximum-flow minimum-cut separates paths that violate distance constraints. SeqAn::T-Coffee aligns the resulting blocks. (PDF p. 3).
The authors propose parallel pairwise searches and parallel alignment of separate blocks as future work. Parallel processing was not presented as an implemented optimization. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Muscle5: High-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased assessments of sequence homology and phylogeny
indicators: The parallel ProbCons implementation applies two consistency transformations by default, constructs a greedy maximum expected accuracy guide tree, and performs 100 randomized refinement rounds. (PDF p. 6).
The perturbation amplitude was selected by trial and error on a Balibase subset. Individual replicate parameters are not optimized against the input sequences. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: HHblits: Lightning-Fast Iterative Protein Sequence Searching by HMM–HMM Alignment
indicators: Viterbi scores determine ranking and statistical significance. Local maximum accuracy alignment instead maximizes the sum of residue-pair probabilities minus the mact penalty. (PDF p. 5).
Matches pass to Viterbi HMM–HMM alignment and maximum accuracy realignment. The default inclusion threshold for adding their sequences is E < 0.001. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: COFFEE: an objective function for multiple sequence alignments
indicators: The authors use the SAGA genetic algorithm to optimize this score. (PDF p. 1).
They propose that pairwise libraries filter noise while retaining information for global optimization. (PDF p. 14).

papers.title: Identification of Common Molecular Subsequences
indicators: Each matrix value represents the maximum similarity of segments that end at its two sequence positions. (PDF p. 1).
Initialize the first row and column to zero. Set H(i,j) to the maximum of H(i−1,j−1)+s(ai,bj), all H(i−k,j)−Wk, all H(i,j−l)−Wl, and zero. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An Icelandic pangenome reference
indicators: Pairwise scoring uses match reward 1, mismatch penalty 4, soft-clip penalty 6, gap-open penalty 7, and gap-extension penalty 1. The maximum weighted haplotype score selects the primary alignment. (PDF p. 10).

papers.title: Protein 3D Structure Computed from Evolutionary Sequence Variation
indicators: EVfold infers residue couplings from multiple sequence alignments with a maximum entropy model. It converts these couplings into distance constraints for protein structure generation. (PDF p. 3).
The study aims to assess the structural information in evolutionary couplings. It does not aim to optimize performance across all available prediction methods. (PDF p. 15).

papers.title: String editing under pattern constraints
indicators: Find minimum-cost edit scripts transforming a string while ensuring intermediate or final substrings satisfy regular constraints. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Iterative Coding Scheme Satisfying GC Balance and Run-Length Constraints for DNA Storage With Robustness to Error Propagation
indicators: For maximum run-length 3, the mapping converts 11 bits into 6 nucleotides. Its information density is 1.8333 bits/nt. (PDF p. 4).
Generate DNA with maximum run-length m and GC ratio within 0.5 ± α, with adjustable constraint values. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast string matching with k differences
indicators: The authors separate pattern preprocessing from text analysis. Both versions use O(nk²) text-analysis time. (PDF p. 3).
The simpler quadratic preprocessing version can be useful when preprocessing occurs in advance or one pattern is searched across many texts. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Time Efficient Algorithm for Finding Longest Common Subsequence from two Molecular Sequences
indicators: The authors exclude bucket construction from repeated query cost because the stored database sequence requires this preprocessing only once. (PDF p. 4).
Find_LCS stores the query index, nucleotide, and candidate database position in a queue. It selects candidates using a pointer and bucket flags. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Rapid and Sensitive Protein Similarity Searches
indicators: Filtering matches by shared diagonal offsets avoids computing the full dynamic programming matrix. (PDF p. 2).
A lookup table identifies exact matches of length ktup between query and database sequences. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A survey of sequence alignment algorithms for next-generation sequencing
indicators: Li and Homer explain alignment indexes, seeding, extension, and their use with different sequencing data. (PDF p. 2).
Fully sensitive MAQ and SeqMap seed schemes require a number of templates that grows exponentially with the mismatch limit. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: An Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence and Substring Problem for Multiple Strings
indicators: When all endpoint symbols match, the recurrence decrements every index and adds one to the previous length. (PDF p. 16).

Interpretation: the return statement leaves the endpoint convention unclear. Under inclusive indexing, a substring of maxLength ending at lastIndexOnY1 starts at lastIndexOnY1 − maxLength + 1. (PDF p. 17).

papers.title: New Processor Array Architectures for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The arrays support preprocessing and subsequence computation on the same architecture. (PDF p. 1).
The execution-time model adds preprocessing, computation, and communication costs. Communication includes startup time and transmission time per word. (PDF p. 15).

papers.title: Algorithms for Jumbled Indexing, Jumbled Border and Jumbled Square on run-length encoded strings
indicators: The authors study jumbled indexing, borders, and squares on run-length encoded strings. Jumble matching requires equal symbol histograms. (PDF p. 2).
Build an index that returns all substrings whose histograms equal a query histogram. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A coarse-grained multicomputer parallel algorithm for the sequential substring constrained longest common subsequence problem
indicators: For overlapping partitions, preprocessing also finds valid suffix-prefix overlap lengths for adjacent constraints. The dynamic program uses separate states for general solutions and solutions that end at a constraint. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Next-Generation Sequence Assembly: Four Stages of Data Processing and Computational Challenges
indicators: The authors organize next-generation sequence assembly into four stages: preprocessing filtering, graph construction, graph simplification, and postprocessing filtering. (PDF p. 1).
Suffix tree or suffix array filters count substrings of variable length. They seek similar candidates for rare substrings and remove affected reads when correction candidates are absent. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Approximating the Longest Common Subsequence problem within a sub-polynomial factor in linear time
indicators: To obtain linear time, the proof first samples an index set U at rate n^{−o(1)}. It applies the reduction to xU and yU. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Protein-to-genome alignment with miniprot
indicators: Miniprot maps proteins to complete genomes with a seed-chain-extend algorithm and spliced dynamic programming. (PDF p. 2).
Genome positions use 256-base bins and 32-bit integers. This avoids the larger index required by 64-bit positions for a human genome. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast Algorithms for the Shortest Unique Palindromic Substring Problem on Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: Preprocessing uses run-length encoded versions of Manacher's maximal palindrome algorithm and the eertree data structure. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Approximate Multiple Pattern String Matching using Bit Parallelism: A Review
indicators: The paper describes BNDM for single-pattern search and a Shift OR filter for multiple-pattern search. (PDF p. 2).
The authors report lower search times for their multiple-pattern Shift OR implementation than for Aho–Corasick. The filter also reports more matches, which require verification. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast text searching: allowing errors
indicators: Partition filtering produces fewer accidental exact matches with a large alphabet. Small alphabets increase such matches and reduce its effectiveness. (PDF p. 7).
A partition-based filtering search accelerates approximate matching by using exact matches. Its performance depends on alphabet size. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: MMseqs2 supports protein sequence searches and iterative profile searches. It combines similar-k-mer filtering, vectorized ungapped alignment, and gapped Smith-Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 1).
The authors argue that consecutive similar 7-mer matches on one diagonal provide a selective filter. Homologues can preserve this pattern, but chance matches rarely do. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Strobealign: flexible seed size enables ultra-fast and accurate read alignment
indicators: The author introduces strobealign, a short-read aligner based on variable-size syncmer and randstrobe seeding. (PDF p. 2).
The E-hits metric is formulated to quantify and minimize seed repetitiveness across reference genomes. (PDF p. 25).

papers.title: A*PA2: Up to 19× Faster Exact Global Alignment
indicators: A*PA2-full adds incremental doubling and the gap-chaining seed heuristic with pre-pruning. The benchmark uses exact seed matches, seed length 12, and a lookahead of 14 seeds. (PDF p. 13).
Pre-pruning removes many off-path seed matches before the main computation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Fast Bit-Vector Algorithm for Approximate String Matching Based on Dynamic Programming
indicators: The author aims to improve verification algorithms for both direct searches and filter-based searches that require candidate verification. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Bilingual language model for protein sequence and structure
indicators: The dataset construction combines sequence clustering, structure clustering, and quality filtering. The final set contains 17 million proteins and supplies 34 million directional translation examples. (PDF p. 2).
Inverse-folding filtering allows up to 10 attempts to reach 70% roundtrip 3Di identity and retains the candidate with the highest roundtrip accuracy. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: The open-closed mod-minimizer algorithm
indicators: The authors introduce the open-closed mod-minimizer algorithm to sample k-mers from DNA strings at reduced density. (PDF p. 1).
Construct robust, low-density seed sampling schemes that improve upon random minimizers for sequence comparison. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A survey of sequence-to-graph mapping algorithms in the pangenome era
indicators: The authors explain sequence-to-graph mapping through seeding, filtering, extension, and alternative methods. (PDF p. 2).
Branches, cycles, and nested cycles make seed extension difficult. These structures arise from multiple alleles and repetitive regions. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: Levenshtein Distance, Sequence Comparison and Biological Database Search
indicators: Database preprocessing can accelerate existing search tools while retaining their sequence-comparison optimizations. (PDF p. 11).
The authors cite prior work that reports orders-of-magnitude acceleration for genomic, protein, and metagenomic BLAST variants after database preprocessing. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: An Improved Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm for Reducing Memory Complexity in Global Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: Preprocessing constructs four bounds from character-equality points. These bounds restrict the region needed during traceback. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Deep embedding and alignment of protein sequences
indicators: Training combines masked language modeling on UniRef50, alignment learning from Pfam-A seed, and homology classification. Random flanks extend Pfam domains to create local alignment examples. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Variation Graph Toolkit Improves Read Mapping by Representing Genetic Variation in the Reference
indicators: GCSA2 indexes paths to locate Maximal Exact Matches (MEMs) for seed-and-extend graph dynamic programming. (PDF p. 8).
Compressed suffix arrays and multithreaded seed clustering permit scaling to gigabase-scale genomes. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Algorithms for Computing the Longest Parameterized Common Subsequence
indicators: Find the maximum common subsequence length under bounds on successive index distances and on the difference between these distances in the two strings. (PDF p. 3).
FIG, ELAG, RIFIG, and RELAG are special cases of LPCS. Setting D = 0 requires equal index distances in both strings. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Constrained Longest Common Subsequences with Run-Length-Encoded Strings
indicators: Use an inverted index of symbol occurrences to derive recurrence values on cuboid faces. (PDF p. 3).
Maintain b-interval and s-interval sets to find the critical index for a DP element. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: Sassy: fuzzy searching DNA sequences using SIMD
indicators: Sassy reports all occurrences of a pattern within a text under edit distance without requiring an offline index. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Improving the Worst Case Performance of the Hunt-Szymanski Strategy for the Longest Common Subsequence of Two Strings
indicators: The algorithm uses standard preprocessing and finger trees. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: SAFARI: pangenome alignment of ancient DNA using
indicators: SAFARI uses a purine/pyrimidine (RY) encoding scheme and an ancillary RYmer index to rescue deaminated reads. (PDF p. 3).
Standard minimizer seeds fail to match in ancient DNA due to terminal deamination damage. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Compressed Dictionary Matching on Run-Length Encoded Strings
indicators: Compressed sorting and compact trie construction preprocess k patterns in O(R_P + k log log k) expected time and O(R_P) space. (PDF p. 3).
After deterministic preprocessing, text parsing and occurrence reporting take O(R_S log log R_P + occ) time. (PDF p. 14).

papers.title: Efficient seeding for error-prone sequences with SubseqHash2
indicators: The authors report 10–50-fold acceleration over SubseqHash while retaining nearly the same seed accuracy. (PDF p. 1).
The study aims to reduce the cost of repeated subsequence seeding while retaining high sensitivity and precision. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: End-to-end learning of multiple sequence alignments
indicators: The study aims to learn alignments jointly with downstream models instead of fixing alignments during preprocessing. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Bit-parallel sequence-to-graph alignment
indicators: The merge algorithm calculates score differences in parallel chunks. It builds comparison masks and a picking mask to form the elementwise minimum of two encoded columns. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Efficient mapping of accurate long reads in minimizer space with mapquik
indicators: They propose long minimizer-space seeds to obtain specific matches without requiring a long contiguous exact match. (PDF p. 2).
Current uses include locating HiFi reads, sorting reads by genomic position, separating reads by chromosome, and filtering nonhuman reads. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: BLAT—The BLAST-Like Alignment Tool
indicators: Indexing the genome lets BLAT scan the shorter query instead of scanning the complete database for each query. The author identifies this as the main source of speed. (PDF p. 10).
With independent letters, the probability of detecting a homologous region with one perfect seed is P = 1 − (1 − M^K)^floor(H/K). M is identity and H is region length. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Pangenome graph construction from genome alignments with Minigraph-Cactus
indicators: Cactus joins exact matching bases into a sequence graph. It uses cactus-graph topology to filter short suspect chains, then aligns unaligned sequences between shared anchors. (PDF p. 4).
The graphs omit interchromosomal events and cannot support centromere studies. The authors identify graph updates and reduced dependence on heuristic filtering as future work. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: Haplotype-aware sequence alignment to pangenome graphs
indicators: Haplotype-aware alignment takes O(|Q||E||H|) time. Chaining takes O(|H|N log(|H|N)) time after O(|E||H|) graph preprocessing. (PDF p. 3).
Each alignment path records graph vertices and selected haplotype indices. A change in haplotype index counts as a recombination. Every graph vertex and edge must have haplotype support. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: GPU-accelerated homology search with MMseqs2
indicators: MMseqs2-GPU performs gapless filtering and gapped protein alignment on GPUs with position-specific scoring matrices. (PDF p. 1).
The authors argue that gapless filtering suits GPUs because it has few data dependencies and avoids the branching and random memory access of k-mer index searches. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: The design and construction of reference pangenome graphs with minigraph
indicators: Sequence assemblies are mapped to an evolving bidirected graph using minimizer chaining and graph alignment. (PDF p. 16).
Minimizer-based distance indexing allows rapid co-linear chaining across graph nodes. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: CREMSA: compressed indexing of (ultra) large multiple sequence alignments
indicators: A 65 GB SARS-CoV-2 alignment becomes a 22 MB disk index that occupies 76 MB in main memory. (PDF p. 10).
Implement the index in C++ with sdsl-lite v3. Use SD bit vectors when the run fraction is below 0.1 and RRR bit vectors otherwise. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Rapid, accurate long- and short-read mapping to large pangenome graphs with vg Giraffe
indicators: The algorithm uses minimizer seeds, zip code distance trees, and anchor chaining across graph topologies. (PDF p. 17).
Dense nested graph variants increase index memory requirements and chaining time. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Edit distance for a run-length-encoded string and an uncompressed string
indicators: Inverted lists retain the largest eligible index for A and B and the smallest eligible index for C. UpdateInvertedLists updates them in constant time as the column advances. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Functional protein mining with conformal guarantees
indicators: The framework supports functional annotation, enzyme classification, and database filtering before structural alignment. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: PLMSearch: Protein language model powers accurate and fast sequence search for remote homology
indicators: Pfam clan matching gives higher recall than Pfam family matching. The authors therefore prefer clans for initial filtering. (PDF p. 6).
An ablation test uses 110 queries with no detected Pfam domain. PLMSearch then gives the same results as SS-predictor because the clan filter retains all pairs. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Fast and accurate multiple-protein-sequence alignment at scale with FAMSA2
indicators: The stochastic medoid algorithm approximates guide trees. Reduced randomness in seed selection improves stability relative to fully random methods such as PartTree. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: On the Complexity of Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: Initialization and insertion propagation each take O(|V| + |E|) time per layer. This gives O(m(|V| + |E|)) time before preprocessing. (PDF p. 12).
The linear-gap algorithm computes the optimal alignment cost in O(|V| + m|E|) time and O(|V|) space under the constant-alphabet preprocessing assumption. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: Fast and Accurate Short Read Alignment with Burrows–Wheeler Transform
indicators: Exact backward search counts matches in O(m) time for a read of length m. It updates suffix array intervals without storing the explicit prefix trie. (PDF p. 2).
Inexact search explores matches, mismatches, insertions, and deletions through suffix array intervals. A reverse-reference BWT computes D in linear time in read length. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Minimap2: Pairwise Alignment for Nucleotide Sequences
indicators: Minimap2 maps nucleotide sequences with minimizer seeds, anchor chaining, and optional base-level alignment. (PDF p. 2).
The author argues that fixed-length hash-table seeds are efficient for long noisy sequences. Multiple seed hits permit repetitive seeds to be skipped. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: MMseqs2 searches protein sequence sets through k-mer filtering, ungapped alignment, and vectorized Smith–Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 1).
The authors identify random main-memory access as a bottleneck for speed and multicore scaling. Their filtering design moves repeated diagonal checks into CPU cache. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Fast and Practical Bit-Vector Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: Preprocessing builds a match vector for each alphabet symbol. A bit is one exactly where that symbol occurs in the shorter string. (PDF p. 4).
Match-vector preprocessing can restrict attention to symbols present in the shorter string when the alphabet is large. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Gapped BLAST and PSI-BLAST: A New Generation of Protein Database Search Programs
indicators: Gapped extension uses dynamic programming in both directions from a seed. It retains cells whose optimal local score is no more than Xg below the best score found. (PDF p. 5).
The seed is the central residue pair in the highest-scoring length-11 segment of the triggering HSP. Shorter HSPs use a central residue pair. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Exact global alignment using A* with chaining seed heuristic and match pruning
indicators: Its seed heuristics combine ordered matches, gap costs, and one-edit matches. Match pruning and diagonal transition reduce search work. (PDF p. 2).
Improve seed heuristic accuracy for long sequences with errors while preserving alignment correctness. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: A New Bucket-Based Algorithm for Finding LCS from two given Molecular Sequences
indicators: Bucket_Collection stores each database index in the bucket for its nucleotide. Each bucket entry has a position and a Boolean flag. (PDF p. 1).
Find_LCS records the query index, nucleotide, and first unflagged matching bucket position beyond Ptr in a queue. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Improved Tools for Biological Sequence Comparison
indicators: FASTA uses a lookup table to find runs of ktup identities. It selects ten diagonal regions, rescores them with a substitution matrix, and retains their highest scoring subregions. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Faster algorithms for RNA-folding using the Four-Russians method
indicators: Simplify Four-Russians preprocessing and its correctness analysis by completing preprocessing before the main computation. (PDF p. 1).
The Frid–Gusfield method can repeat preprocessing for the same horizontal vector. Indexing by both vectors prevents this duplicate work. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: An Analysis on Computation of Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm
indicators: A coordinate function maps each multidimensional index to linear memory. It repeatedly multiplies the accumulated index by the next sequence length and adds that coordinate. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
indicators: Forward–Backward first computes posterior alignment probabilities from combined 3Di and amino acid substitution scores. The method extends the ten highest-scoring aligned 7-mers and retains three seed anchors. (PDF p. 2).
For each seed, the method recomputes LoL-scores and posterior probabilities. It adds residue pairs above a probability threshold to the anchor set until convergence. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Matching Sequences under Deletion/Insertion Constraints
indicators: Find a longest common subsequence subject to a bound on its deletion/insertion index. (PDF p. 2).
The author presents the DI index as a genetically meaningful alternative to arbitrarily selected numerical criteria. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Bounded Weighted Edit Distance
indicators: The authors give a dynamic algorithm for bounded weighted edit distance with arbitrary normalized edit costs. A fixed threshold k controls preprocessing and update costs. (PDF p. 1).
The algorithm uses Õ(nk^γ) preprocessing and Õ(k^(3−γ)) time per update, for γ in [0,1]. It returns infinity when the distance exceeds k. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Mugsy: fast multiple alignment of closely related whole genomes
indicators: Nucmer searches all genome pairs. Delta-filter retains matches in the highest-scoring chains of both sequences for multiple alignment. Scores combine match length with squared sequence identity. (PDF p. 3).
A modified delta-filter reports duplicated segments found in the chain of only one sequence. Mugsy saves these separately in MAF format. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: COFFEE: an objective function for multiple sequence alignments
indicators: They propose that pairwise libraries filter noise while retaining information for global optimization. (PDF p. 14).
The library is stored in a lookup table for evaluation. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Ultrafast and Memory-Efficient Alignment of Short DNA Sequences to the Human Genome
indicators: The Burrows-Wheeler transform and FM-index enable memory-efficient exact matching with compact index representation. (PDF p. 2).
The reference genome is indexed using a checkpointed FM-index over the Burrows-Wheeler transformed sequence. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Efficient CGM-based parallel algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem with multiple substring-exclusion constraints
indicators: The sequential preprocessing removes duplicate constraints and proper superstrings of other forbidden constraints. These removals preserve the required exclusion conditions. (PDF p. 4).
Parallel preprocessing assigns alphabet subsets to processors for transition-table computation. An all-to-all communication step then shares the results. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Opportunistic Data Structures with Applications
indicators: For text length U and pattern length p, the index reports occ occurrences in O(p + occ log^ε U) time for any fixed ε > 0. Storage is O(H_k(T)) + o(1) bits per symbol for fixed k. (PDF p. 2).
The paper extends the index to dynamic text collections and proposes its use in Compressed Glimpse. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Review on Sequence Alignment Algorithms for Short Reads Based on Next-Generation Sequencing
indicators: SOAP uses seed extension and a hash lookup table. The described search allows one continuous gap or up to two mismatches. (PDF p. 6).
The authors report that FM-index methods generally run faster and align more reads than hash-based methods in their comparison. (PDF p. 10).

papers.title: Efficient algorithms for the longest common subsequence in k-length substrings
indicators: They give dynamic programming, sparse, dense, and tabulation algorithms. All use linear-time preprocessing to find matching length-k substrings. (PDF p. 1).
The dense analysis separates rows by match density. It balances preprocessing costs with block size b = √t₂ and threshold t₂ = (k log n)^(2/3). (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Label-guided seed-chain-extend alignment on annotated De Bruijn graphs
indicators: Seeds of length l ≤ k match graph-node suffixes. Each anchor records the query position, seed length, node, and label. (PDF p. 3).
Graph preprocessing replaces a full traversal-distance matrix with additional walks that span discarded edges. Coordinate graph annotations encode these walks without loss. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Lossless pangenome indexing using tag arrays
indicators: The method adds run-length-compressed graph-coordinate tags to an FM-index of haplotypes. Queries report distinct matching graph positions. (PDF p. 3).
