Sampled tag arrays and an r-index also support coordinate translation between haplotypes that share graph paths. (PDF p. 20).

papers.title: GraphAligner: Rapid and Versatile Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: GraphAligner aligns long reads to sequence graphs with a seed-and-extend method and bit-parallel banded dynamic programming. (PDF p. 9).
The minimizer seeding strategy relies on long reads spanning simple graph regions. Short reads can remain entirely within regions with dense variation. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Next-Generation Sequence Assembly: Four Stages of Data Processing and Computational Challenges
indicators: Early error correction can reduce graph size. Correction during graph simplification can address errors that become visible only after graph construction. (PDF p. 3).
The authors state that parallel error correction during graph construction can reduce total computation time. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Strobealign: flexible seed size enables ultra-fast and accurate read alignment
indicators: Speed up short-read alignment to large eukaryotic genomes while maintaining high tolerance for sequencing errors. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Codes With Run-Length and GC-Content Constraints for DNA-Based Data Storage
indicators: The authors identify homopolymer length and GC-content as factors that affect DNA synthesis and sequencing errors. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Iterative Coding Scheme Satisfying GC Balance and Run-Length Constraints for DNA Storage With Robustness to Error Propagation
indicators: The intended application is constrained DNA data storage. The authors also propose screening for unwanted patterns, such as primers. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Protein remote homology detection and structural alignment using deep learning
indicators: The GPU implementation batches differentiable alignments. The authors report runtime about ten times faster than the naive CPU implementation. (PDF p. 13).
Encoding 50,000 queries took up to 40 minutes on one GPU. Searching their vectors against five million proteins took under 20 seconds. Encoding was the search bottleneck. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: SAUTE: sequence assembly using target enrichment
indicators: The tool uses target sequences as seeds to construct localized de Bruijn graphs without whole-genome assembly. (PDF p. 2).
Targeted local assembly avoids the computational burden and misassemblies of de novo whole-genome assembly. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: WFA-GPU: gap-affine pairwise read-alignment using GPUs
indicators: The authors present WFA-GPU, a GPU-accelerated pairwise sequence aligner based on the wavefront alignment algorithm. (PDF p. 1).
WFA-GPU adapts wavefront operations to GPU hardware using 16-base block comparisons and memory-coalesced diagonals. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: A survey of sequence alignment algorithms for next-generation sequencing
indicators: For the SNP test, simulated chromosome 6 reads are mapped to the whole genome. SAMtools calls and filters SNPs, and one configuration uses GATK realignment. (PDF p. 6).
The authors report typical Bowtie and BWA throughput of approximately 7 Gbp per CPU day, compared with approximately 3 Gbp for the Illumina base caller. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: A trimodal protein language model enables advanced protein searches
indicators: Training combines 14 million Swiss-Prot protein–text pairs with 25 million filtered TrEMBL50 pairs. An initial model filters a pool of 300 million noisy pairs. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: New Processor Array Architectures for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The first architecture implements dynamic programming matrices c and LCS with bit-parallel operations. The second processes the bit-level algorithm in blocks. (PDF p. 18).

papers.title: A coarse-grained multicomputer parallel algorithm for the sequential substring constrained longest common subsequence problem
indicators: When p ≤ l, each processor receives one parallel plane. When p > l, a snake-like mapping assigns several processors to a parallel plane. (PDF p. 7).
Three-dimensional partitioning reduces block size. The authors identify l mod p = 0 as the best partitioning case because all parallel planes have equal size. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Longest common subsequence between run-length-encoded strings: a new algorithm with improved parallelism
indicators: The authors derive O(mN + Mn − mn) computation and O(m + n) parallel steps with M + N systolic units. M and N are string lengths; m and n are run counts. (PDF p. 6).
The authors relate the parallel speedup to the RLE compression factor. They also expect a similar reduction in memory transfer time. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Fast and Flexible String Matching by Combining Bit-parallelism and Suffix Automata
indicators: The authors introduce Backward Nondeterministic Dawg Matching (BNDM). It combines suffix automata with bit-parallel simulation. (PDF p. 3).
The authors identify a limitation of earlier bit-parallel methods: they support flexible patterns but cannot skip text characters. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: BIMSA: accelerating long sequence alignment using processing-in-memory
indicators: Comparators are CPU WFA2lib, WFA-GPU, and AIM implementations of Needleman–Wunsch, WFA, and adaptive WFA. (PDF p. 6).
AIM-WFA cannot process the tested sequences of 10,000 bases or longer because of memory limits. WFA-GPU is up to 1.8 times faster than BIMSA on the 10,000-base tests. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Parallel Algorithm for Longest Common Subsequence in a String
indicators: The authors propose a parallel dynamic programming algorithm for LCS. The C implementation uses OpenMP. (PDF p. 3).
The authors give space complexity as Θ(MN) for the symbol and weight matrices. Parallel execution does not reduce this storage requirement. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Accurate Prediction of Protein Structures and Interactions Using a Three-Track Neural Network
indicators: For proteins longer than 400 residues, the pyRosetta route requires 8 GB of GPU memory instead of 24 GB for the end-to-end route. It adds CPU structure-modeling work. (PDF p. 4).
After sequence and template search, backbone prediction for proteins shorter than 400 residues takes about 10 minutes on an RTX2080 GPU. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Optimal Gap-Affine Alignment in O(s) Space
indicators: Table 1 reports simulated sequences from 10 Kbp to 2 Mbp at 10% and 20% error. It measures execution time per million aligned bases and memory use. (PDF p. 5).
For simulated 2 Mbp sequences at 20% error, Table 1 reports 1,429.0 seconds per million aligned bases and 267 MB for BiWFA. WFA-high and wfalm fail in this condition. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: The authors searched 1.1 billion predicted proteins against 16479 Pfam profiles. The search produced 370 million domain annotations with E-values below 0.001. (PDF p. 2).

The benchmark used 6370 queries, 3.4 million UniProt database sequences, and 27 million reversed sequences. Query regions without annotations were scrambled while preserving local amino acid composition. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Accelerating Cryptanalysis with the Method of Four Russians
indicators: The model places the crossover between M4RI and Strassen-based inversion at approximately 6.65 million rows. (PDF p. 3).
Attack runtime estimates ignore sparsity and use an approximate conversion from floating-point throughput to matrix memory-operation throughput. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: Next Generation Sequence Analysis and Computational Genomics Using Graphical Pipeline Workflows
indicators: The system targets researchers who analyze whole-genome, exome, and targeted sequencing data. (PDF p. 22).
Simulation uses dwgsim from DNAA v0.1.2 to generate 30 million reads of 100 bases from hg18. It uses default parameters and the default empirical error model. (PDF p. 23).

papers.title: Bilingual language model for protein sequence and structure
indicators: The dataset construction combines sequence clustering, structure clustering, and quality filtering. The final set contains 17 million proteins and supplies 34 million directional translation examples. (PDF p. 2).
Training uses DeepSpeed stage 2, gradient accumulation, bf16 precision, and torchInductor to increase throughput. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A survey of sequence-to-graph mapping algorithms in the pangenome era
indicators: PaSGAL uses SIMD and a three-phase parallel approach for base-level alignment. (PDF p. 16).
Many parallel optimizations depend on specific hardware. Moving them to another platform can require substantial redesign. (PDF p. 21).

papers.title: MUSCLE: a multiple sequence alignment method with reduced time and space complexity
indicators: It introduces MUSCLE-fast for high-throughput use and a protocol to evaluate profile alignment functions. (PDF p. 1).
MUSCLE-fast targets high-throughput alignment with a speed and accuracy trade-off. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An nf-core framework for the systematic comparison of alternative modeling tools: the multiple sequence alignment case study
indicators: The framework separates guide tree computation, alignment assembly, and evaluation. It can run alternative tools and parameter settings in parallel. (PDF p. 3).
Toolsheets permit parallel comparison of tool parameters and guide tree choices. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Multiple sequence alignment with the Clustal series of programs
indicators: Clustal builds a multiple alignment through successive pairwise alignments in guide-tree order. The original implementation combined progressive alignment with memory-efficient dynamic programming. (PDF p. 1).
Parallel ClustalW and ClustalX implementations reportedly achieved speed increases of up to tenfold on 16 CPUs. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Variation Graph Toolkit Improves Read Mapping by Representing Genetic Variation in the Reference
indicators: Make variation graphs practical as references for gigabase-scale genomic resequencing without reference bias. (PDF p. 2).
Compressed suffix arrays and multithreaded seed clustering permit scaling to gigabase-scale genomes. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Fast, accurate construction of multiple sequence alignments from protein language embeddings
indicators: Runtime scaling has a log-scale slope of 1.01 when the smallest subset is excluded. The 95% confidence interval is 0.798–1.216. (PDF p. 11).
Reciprocal-weight improvements saturate near 800. ESM-2 with 650 million parameters performs best among the four tested PLMs. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: Accelign: a GPU-based library for accelerating pairwise sequence alignment
indicators: The authors report peak global-alignment throughput of 16.1 TCUPS with linear gaps and 9.1 TCUPS with affine gaps on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. (PDF p. 1).
The authors aim to generalize their GPU parallelization method across sequence types, scoring schemes, and alignment classes. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Sassy: fuzzy searching DNA sequences using SIMD
indicators: The algorithm uses SIMD-parallel bit-parallel dynamic programming over 4-letter DNA alphabets. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Rewriting protein alphabets with language models
indicators: Clustering and remote homology detection in massive protein databases including the AlphaFold Database. (PDF p. 7).
TEA is evaluated on SCOPe benchmark alignments and 15.3 million AFDB cluster representatives. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Efficient seeding for error-prone sequences with SubseqHash2
indicators: SIMD reduces the stated runtime to O(Nnk) when d states fit the supported parallel computation. The reported supported range extends to d = 32. (PDF p. 3).

Pairwise tests used 10 simulated sequence pairs at each error rate of 5%, 10%, and 15%. Initial sequences had one million bases. Metrics measured character coverage by true and false seed matches. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Multiple protein structure alignment at scale with FoldMason
indicators: Progressive alignment merges structure profiles from the leaves to the root. Independent alignments at each tree rank run in parallel. (PDF p. 2).
FoldMason uses striped accelerated ungapped alignment for initial comparisons and parallel progressive alignment for profile merging. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Bit-parallel sequence-to-graph alignment
indicators: Use bit-parallel operations for exact matching and semi-global alignment on directed graphs with character-labeled nodes. (PDF p. 2).
The merge algorithm calculates score differences in parallel chunks. It builds comparison masks and a picking mask to form the elementwise minimum of two encoded columns. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Sequential and Parallel Algorithms for the All-Substrings Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present sequential and parallel algorithms for the all-substrings longest common subsequence problem. (PDF p. 2).
Solve the all-substrings LCS problem efficiently in sequential and distributed parallel environments. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BLAT—The BLAST-Like Alignment Tool
indicators: BLAT searches a genome index for perfect or near-perfect seed matches. It extends candidate regions and joins their alignments into larger gene-scale alignments. (PDF p. 2).

A translated timing test compared BLAT and WU-TBLASTX on 1,000 mouse reads against repeat-masked human chromosome 22. A larger test compared coding-base and exon coverage using 13 million mouse reads. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Coarse-Grained Parallel Algorithm for the All-Substrings Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The authors present a BSP/CGM parallel algorithm for all-substrings longest common subsequence (ALCS). It computes LCS lengths for A and every substring of B. (PDF p. 1).
The authors seek an efficient parallel ALCS algorithm with reduced computation, storage, and communication costs. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Geometric algebra generation of molecular surfaces
indicators: Piecewise initial data assign zero inside atomic spheres and one outside. Gaussian initial data use the maximum of atom-centered Gaussian functions, with a scale parameter of 3 Å. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: GPU-accelerated homology search with MMseqs2
indicators: MMseqs2-GPU performs gapless filtering and gapped protein alignment on GPUs with position-specific scoring matrices. (PDF p. 1).
The benchmarks show faster single-query searches and faster structure prediction workflows. Large-batch performance depends on GPU count. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: The design and construction of reference pangenome graphs with minigraph
indicators: Construct comprehensive reference pangenome graphs from multiple assembled vertebrate genomes at chromosome scale. (PDF p. 1).
Constructs chromosome-scale human pangenome graphs in hours, discovering thousands of non-reference structural variants. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: CREMSA: compressed indexing of (ultra) large multiple sequence alignments
indicators: Improve compression through sequence reordering and enable large-scale covariation analysis. (PDF p. 2).
Average nucleotide access time rises from 28 ns for 10,000 sequences to 111 ns for 1.87 million sequences. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Building pangenome graphs
indicators: Local smoothing removes cycles shorter than the POA scale while preserving larger cycles that represent structural variation. (PDF p. 3).
PGGB can generate phased VCF outputs from whole-genome assemblies, plus graph statistics and visualizations. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improving spliced alignment by modeling splice sites with deep learning
indicators: The authors estimate that a 1% false-positive rate would produce 3.75 million false donor predictions in a mammalian genome. Splice predictions therefore require additional evidence. (PDF p. 14).
The score uses twice the base-2 logarithm of the probability ratio to match the BLOSUM scale used by miniprot. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: An O(ND) Difference Algorithm and Its Variations
indicators: A reported large comparison used two 1.5-million-byte sequences on a VAX 785 running 4.2BSD UNIX. (PDF p. 2).
The two 1.5-million-byte sequences were compared in less than two minutes, with more than 500 differences. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Functional protein mining with conformal guarantees
indicators: The structural search application filters the 2.3 million protein clustered AlphaFold Database before DALI alignment. (PDF p. 7).
DALI searches use parallel batches of 1000 structures. Protein embeddings use one A6000 GPU, and FAISS indexes the embeddings and generates similarity scores. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: AlphaFold and Implications for Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
indicators: For Httex1, large-scale Monte Carlo simulations provide initial ensembles. A Bayesian method reweights them with single-molecule FRET measurements collected at low picomolar concentrations. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Fast and accurate multiple-protein-sequence alignment at scale with FAMSA2
indicators: The authors argue that accurate existing aligners scale poorly beyond thousands of sequences. Larger protein families require faster alignment methods. (PDF p. 2).
Length-based prefiltering reduces pairwise comparisons. Parallel execution operates within LCS calculation and progressive alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and Accurate Short Read Alignment with Burrows–Wheeler Transform
indicators: The authors aim to accelerate large-scale short-read mapping while supporting gaps that MAQ cannot handle in single-end reads. (PDF p. 1).
wgsim generated one million read pairs at each length of 32, 70, and 125 bases. Simulations used 0.09% SNPs, 0.01% indels, and 2% uniform sequencing errors. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: The supplement describes sequence and profile search modes, memory-access optimizations, and parallel execution. (PDF p. 3).
Compute optimal ungapped scores for 32 targets in parallel with AVX2. Pass alignments above 15 bits to vectorized Smith–Waterman alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Theseus: fast and optimal affine-gap sequence-tograph alignment
indicators: Alignment throughput, memory usage, and peak memory consumption are measured across partial order alignment graphs. (PDF p. 8).
A memory-efficient backtrace algorithm recovers optimal alignment paths directly from wavefront checkpoints. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Exact global alignment using A* with chaining seed heuristic and match pruning
indicators: Synthetic experiments use uniform random sequences up to 10 million bases. Runtime scaling is reported at 4% and 12% divergence against EDLIB and BIWFA. (PDF p. 1).
Best-fit runtime scales as n^1.06 at 4% divergence and n^1.24 at 12% divergence. At 10 million bases and 4% divergence, reported speedup exceeds 500-fold over EDLIB and BIWFA. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Rapid and sensitive protein complex alignment with Foldseek-Multimer
indicators: Enable fast structural alignment and search across massive multimeric protein complex databases. (PDF p. 1).
Large-scale clustering and searching of complex structures in the AlphaFold and 3DComplex databases. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast Gap-Affine Pairwise Alignment Using the Wavefront Algorithm
indicators: Real data include 100000 HiSeq reads of 100 bases and 25000 ONT reads. Simulated data use lengths from 100 to 100000 bases and error rates from 1% to 20%, with 10 million bases per dataset. (PDF p. 6).
All experiments use one thread. Multi-threaded execution is discussed as a possible combination with parallel processing of separate alignments. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: A Relative Position based Algorithm to find out the Longest Common Subsequence from Multiple Biological Sequences
indicators: The authors claim O(n) time for the DNA case. They describe parallel runtime as O(K), where K is the time of the slowest processor. (PDF p. 7).
Parallel execution assigns one processor to each alphabet character. The DNA example uses four processors. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Faster algorithms for RNA-folding using the Four-Russians method
indicators: The serial variants take O(n³/log n) time. The parallel method takes O(n²/log n) time with n processes. (PDF p. 6).
The authors implement the parallel method in CUDA and organize memory access around tiles. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
indicators: Within Foldseek, LoL-align can refine leading hits after prefiltering for large-scale structure comparisons. (PDF p. 1).
The AFDB test used 2,000 queries with at least 100 residues at pLDDT ≥ 0.7. Each tool searched up to 2,000 Foldseek hits per query from 2.3 million cluster representatives. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Speeding-up Hirschberg and Hunt-Szymanski LCS Algorithms
indicators: The authors present bit-parallel formulations of the Hirschberg and Hunt-Szymanski LCS algorithms. (PDF p. 1).
Bit-parallel operations allow testing multiple character match states simultaneously within single machine words. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: TM-Vec 2: Accelerated Protein Homology Detection for Structural Similarity
indicators: Compact transformer models with optimized attention can match the structural representation power of 3-billion-parameter PLMs. (PDF p. 3).
High-throughput structural annotation of metagenomic dark matter and viral proteomes. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: M2Align: parallel multiple sequence alignment with a multi-objective metaheuristic
indicators: It stores gap information and evaluates candidate alignments in parallel. Tests on BAliBASE show reduced runtime with up to 20 cores. (PDF p. 2).
Serial profiling of BAliBASE instance BB20001 identifies solution evaluation as the main runtime cost. This motivates parallel evaluation. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Mugsy: fast multiple alignment of closely related whole genomes
indicators: The authors propose parallel pairwise searches and parallel alignment of separate blocks as future work. Parallel processing was not presented as an implemented optimization. (PDF p. 8).
MLAGAN, Pecan, and FSA received blocks defined by Mugsy. These tests compared alignment components rather than independent whole-genome workflows. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Muscle5: High-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased assessments of sequence homology and phylogeny
indicators: The parallel ProbCons implementation applies two consistency transformations by default, constructs a greedy maximum expected accuracy guide tree, and performs 100 randomized refinement rounds. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Ultrafast and Memory-Efficient Alignment of Short DNA Sequences to the Human Genome
indicators: Bowtie aligns over 25 million reads per hour to the human genome using roughly 1.3 GB of memory. (PDF p. 1).
Map massive volumes of next-generation sequencing short reads to mammalian genomes with minimal memory and runtime. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An Icelandic pangenome reference
indicators: HPRC-ICE contains 788 haplotypes and 51.41 million small variants. Weaver produces alignments in reference coordinates for use with existing analysis tools. (PDF p. 1).
The authors select GraphTyper for population genotyping. They estimate that DeepVariant would need over ten million CPU hours for this task. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Efficient CGM-based parallel algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem with multiple substring-exclusion constraints
indicators: The objective is to schedule dependent subproblems without redundant evaluation and obtain efficient parallel execution on p processors. (PDF p. 2).
Parallel preprocessing assigns alphabet subsets to processors for transition-table computation. An all-to-all communication step then shares the results. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: A Review on Sequence Alignment Algorithms for Short Reads Based on Next-Generation Sequencing
indicators: The authors describe short-read mapping through hash tables, FM-indexes, and GPU implementations. (PDF p. 8).

GPU-RMAP transfers genome and read hash tables to GPU memory. It scans independent genome segments in parallel, scores locations, and distributes reads across threads to select the highest scores. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Protein embedding based alignment
indicators: The authors also tested ESM2-T36-3B-UR50D. This model has three billion parameters and produces 2560-dimensional residue vectors. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: A draft human pangenome reference
indicators: The authors report that an associated study stores the pangenomes losslessly in a compressed binary GFA representation of 3–6 GB, despite representing over 282 billion sequence bases. (PDF p. 11).

The draft adds 119 million bases of euchromatic polymorphic sequence and 1,115 gene duplications relative to GRCh38. The abstract reports 34% fewer small-variant discovery errors and 104% more detected structural variants per haplotype. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Lossless pangenome indexing using tag arrays
indicators: Separate chromosome construction controls memory and permits parallel processing. The authors report that parallel chromosome indexing can more than halve wall-clock time. (PDF p. 20).
Tag runs increased from 12.7 billion to 26.2 billion between the two datasets. Final tag array sizes were 68.6 GiB and 149 GiB. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: GraphAligner: Rapid and Versatile Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: GraphAligner aligns long reads to sequence graphs with a seed-and-extend method and bit-parallel banded dynamic programming. (PDF p. 9).
The authors argue that full dynamic programming is unsuitable for aligning many reads to large graphs, even with their earlier bit-parallel acceleration. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Protein remote homology detection and structural alignment using deep learning
indicators: Differentiable Needleman–Wunsch uses logsumexp and softmax to produce an expected traceback matrix. Directional derivatives and local Hessians support training. Cross-entropy compares predicted alignment probabilities with TM-align reference alignments. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: Approximating the Longest Common Subsequence problem within a sub-polynomial factor in linear time
indicators: The author presents a randomized algorithm that estimates LCS within an n^{o(1)} factor in O(n) time, with high probability. (PDF p. 2).
The main theorem gives an O(n)-time n^{o(1)}-factor approximation with high probability. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: A Survey on Sequence Alignment Algorithms and State-of-the-Art Aligners
indicators: The review describes diversity control in quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization as a way to improve global search during profile HMM training. (PDF p. 30).

The review reports that QPSO and its diversity-controlled variant improved benchmark performance for profile HMM training compared with Baum–Welch and classical PSO. The excerpt gives no numerical effect sizes. (PDF p. 30).

papers.title: BAli-Phy version 3: model-based co-estimation of alignment and phylogeny
indicators: The author argues that a posterior distribution of alignments accounts for uncertainty that a single alignment estimate omits. (PDF p. 1).
MCMC samples contain a tree, an alignment, and numerical parameters. Alignment proposals operate with a probabilistic indel model. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Next Generation Sequence Analysis and Computational Genomics Using Graphical Pipeline Workflows
indicators: CNVseq compares read counts in sliding windows between test and reference individuals. ERDS uses a hidden Markov model with expected read depth estimated by expectation maximization and corrected for GC bias. (PDF p. 19).

papers.title: MSAProbs: multiple sequence alignment based on pair hidden Markov models and partition function posterior probabilities
indicators: MSAProbs combines pair-HMM and partition-function posterior probabilities for multiple protein sequence alignment. (PDF p. 1).
It uses weighted probabilistic consistency, weighted profile-profile alignment, and iterative refinement. OpenMP parallelism reduces execution time. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Analysis of Evolutionary Algorithms for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: Theorem 7 bounds the probability of finding an optimum within t fitness evaluations by t·exp(−Ω(n)). It covers all crossover probabilities and polynomial parent and offspring population sizes. (PDF p. 15).
The framework combines elitist plus-selection, uniform crossover, and standard bit mutation. Population sizes and crossover probability define different algorithm instances. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning (Alphafold)
indicators: Splines fitted to negative log distance probabilities form the distance potential. A sequence-independent reference correction, a torsion potential, and a Rosetta steric term complete the objective. (PDF p. 3).
Contact evaluation converts distograms to contact probabilities by summing probability below 8 Å. Comparisons use submissions from groups 032 and 498. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: Robust Deep Learning–Based Protein Sequence Design Using ProteinMPNN
indicators: An autoregressive message-passing graph neural network maps backbone geometry to amino acid probabilities. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Direct-Coupling Analysis of Residue Coevolution Captures Native Contacts Across Many Protein Families
indicators: The study compares direct-information rankings with mutual information and an approximate Bayesian method. The main average uses the structure with the highest true-positive rate for each family. (PDF p. 3).
The average contact rate among the top 20 predictions was 84%. mfDCA exceeded both mutual information and the approximate Bayesian comparator. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Amino Acid Substitution Matrices from Protein Blocks
indicators: Each score is log2 of the observed pair probability divided by its chance expectation. Scores are multiplied by two and rounded to integers. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Methods for Assessing the Statistical Significance of Molecular Sequence Features by Using General Scoring Schemes
indicators: The authors argue that suitable target frequencies should match the composition of the regions being sought. This supports log-likelihood ratio scores. (PDF p. 3).
For independent letters, the model requires a negative expected score and some probability of a positive score. The maximal segment score grows on the order of ln(n)/λ*. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Improving spliced alignment by modeling splice sites with deep learning
indicators: The transformed score compares the empirical probability of a candidate site with a null model that gives all GT or AG sites equal probability. (PDF p. 5).
Calibration divides raw scores into 50 bins by default. Each bin uses annotated and unannotated site counts to estimate an empirical probability. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Functional protein mining with conformal guarantees
indicators: Isotonic regression maps similarity scores to nondecreasing match probabilities. Venn-Abers prediction fits two regressions with hypothetical test labels 0 and 1. (PDF p. 10).

papers.title: AlphaFold and Implications for Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
indicators: For Httex1, large-scale Monte Carlo simulations provide initial ensembles. A Bayesian method reweights them with single-molecule FRET measurements collected at low picomolar concentrations. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: An Evolutionary Model for Maximum Likelihood Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: The authors derive maximum likelihood alignment of two DNA sequences from a statistical model with explicit transition probabilities. (PDF p. 1).
The authors argue that evolutionary event weights should depend on event probabilities. These probabilities depend on the sequence pair. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and accurate multiple-protein-sequence alignment at scale with FAMSA2
indicators: Structural tests used LDDT on about 1,100 AlphaFold families. Evolutionary tests used 1,860 simulated families and agreement between maximum likelihood and minimum evolution trees. (PDF p. 3).
Agreement between maximum likelihood and minimum evolution trees is a proxy. The authors state that greater agreement does not demonstrate greater phylogenetic accuracy. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein Homology Detection by HMM–HMM Comparison
indicators: Profile HMMs represent position-specific insertion and deletion probabilities. The author argues that these probabilities penalize chance matches more than homologous matches. (PDF p. 2).
The score separates into match-column scores and the logarithm of the path transition probability. The column score is log(sum_a q_i(a)p_j(a)/f(a)). (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A Model of Evolutionary Change in Proteins
indicators: The model combines exchange counts and relative mutabilities to estimate replacement probabilities at specified evolutionary distances. (PDF p. 3).
Compare replacement probabilities with chance residue frequencies to obtain relatedness odds. Add log odds across positions to represent the product of position-specific odds. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Hidden Markov Models in Computational Biology: Applications to Protein Modeling
indicators: EF-hand experiments compared training and held-out negative log-likelihood scores. Small training sets caused overfitting, which largely disappeared at about 100 sequences. (PDF p. 28).
The authors use deletion probabilities and amino acid distribution entropy to distinguish conserved and variable regions in the globin model. (PDF p. 21).

papers.title: Fast, Scalable Generation of High-Quality Protein Multiple Sequence Alignments Using Clustal Omega
indicators: Clustal Omega combines a scalable guide tree method with profile HMM alignment to construct protein MSAs. (PDF p. 2).
mBed converts sequences to distance vectors for rapid clustering. HHalign then aligns profile hidden Markov models during progressive alignment. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Profile Hidden Markov Models
indicators: Profile HMMs convert multiple sequence alignments into probabilistic scoring models for remote homology searches. (PDF p. 1).
The author examines recent advances in profile HMM methods, with emphasis on alternative architectures, model libraries, and fold recognition. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
indicators: Forward–Backward first computes posterior alignment probabilities from combined 3Di and amino acid substitution scores. The method extends the ten highest-scoring aligned 7-mers and retains three seed anchors. (PDF p. 2).
For each seed, the method recomputes LoL-scores and posterior probabilities. It adds residue pairs above a probability threshold to the anchor set until convergence. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: ProbCons: Probabilistic Consistency-Based Multiple Sequence Alignment
indicators: ProbCons constructs progressive protein multiple sequence alignments with pair-HMM posterior probabilities and probabilistic consistency. (PDF p. 2).
The study aims to improve alignment quality through a scoring function that combines posterior probabilities with three-way consistency. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Muscle5: High-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased assessments of sequence homology and phylogeny
indicators: A double-affine-gap HMM computes posterior probabilities for residue pairs. The model uses separate states for short and long gaps and BLOSUM62-based protein emission probabilities. (PDF p. 6).
HMM probabilities change by P → (1 + αδ)P, with δ uniform from −1 to 1. The default α is 0.25. Probabilities are then normalized within mutually exclusive event sets. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: HHblits: Lightning-Fast Iterative Protein Sequence Searching by HMM–HMM Alignment
indicators: Viterbi scores determine ranking and statistical significance. Local maximum accuracy alignment instead maximizes the sum of residue-pair probabilities minus the mact penalty. (PDF p. 5).
Database HMM columns are mapped to 219 representative profile columns. This approximation omits HMM insertion and deletion probabilities. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Protein 3D Structure Computed from Evolutionary Sequence Variation
indicators: The maximum entropy model fits pair frequencies from an aligned protein family while keeping sequence probabilities maximally even under those constraints. (PDF p. 3).

The authors compare global direct information and Bayesian network models with local mutual information and statistical coupling analysis. They also generate structures from Bayesian network constraints for ten proteins. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: Approximating the Longest Common Subsequence problem within a sub-polynomial factor in linear time
indicators: The author presents a randomized algorithm that estimates LCS within an n^{o(1)} factor in O(n) time, with high probability. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BAli-Phy version 3: model-based co-estimation of alignment and phylogeny
indicators: BAli-Phy uses MCMC to jointly estimate alignment, phylogeny, and evolutionary parameters from unaligned sequences. (PDF p. 1).
MCMC samples contain a tree, an alignment, and numerical parameters. Alignment proposals operate with a probabilistic indel model. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Protein Structure Comparison by Alignment of Distance Matrices
indicators: The method identifies contact patterns and aligns them using Monte Carlo optimization. (PDF p. 1).
Hexapeptide fragment pairs with similar distance patterns are assembled using Monte Carlo search. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: An O(ND) Difference Algorithm and Its Variations
indicators: The abstract states O(N + D²) expected time under a basic stochastic model, with N denoting total input length. (PDF p. 1).
The expected-time bound depends on a stochastic model. It is not presented as an unconditional runtime guarantee. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: AlphaFold and Implications for Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
indicators: For Httex1, large-scale Monte Carlo simulations provide initial ensembles. A Bayesian method reweights them with single-molecule FRET measurements collected at low picomolar concentrations. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Profile Analysis: Detection of Distantly Related Proteins
indicators: The authors propose libraries of family profiles to infer structural motifs. They also propose profile scores based on hydrophobicity, secondary structure preference, or side-chain volume. (PDF p. 4).
The authors present structural motif inference as a possible future use. The reported experiments test family detection. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Hidden Markov Models in Computational Biology: Applications to Protein Modeling
indicators: The authors train HMMs on unaligned sequences to model globins, kinase catalytic domains, and EF-hand motifs. (PDF p. 1).
The EF-hand search suggested a motif in a conserved intracellular region of L-type calcium channels. The authors present this as a proposed biological interpretation. (PDF p. 30).

papers.title: String editing under pattern constraints
indicators: Constrained string editing models biological sequence modifications that must preserve functional motifs or structural sites. (PDF p. 2).
Biosequence engineering, motif-preserving alignment, and formal language-constrained sequence transformation. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Automated assembly of protein blocks for database searching
indicators: The path score sums each block score multiplied by its merged-motif count. It then multiplies this sum by the fraction of sequences included in the path. (PDF p. 2).
Modified MOTIF finds three-residue motifs with two spacing values. Sequence shuffling sets the significance threshold, and the system retains the 50 highest-scoring motif blocks. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Identification of Direct Residue Contacts in Protein–Protein Interaction by Message Passing
indicators: The authors combine covariance analysis with global statistical inference to distinguish direct residue couplings from indirect correlations. (PDF p. 1).
The SK/RR analysis separated nine pairs with high mutual and direct information from 22 pairs with high mutual information but weak direct coupling. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: CREMSA: compressed indexing of (ultra) large multiple sequence alignments
indicators: Improve compression through sequence reordering and enable large-scale covariation analysis. (PDF p. 2).
Compute column entropy and pairwise G-test and RNAalifold scores to examine conservation and covariation. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Protein 3D Structure Computed from Evolutionary Sequence Variation
indicators: The authors argue that local correlation measures cannot separate direct coupling from transitive correlation. A global model addresses interdependencies among residue pairs. (PDF p. 3).

Mean field direct coupling analysis estimates residue couplings. Selected couplings become distance constraints for distance geometry, energy minimization, and molecular dynamics refinement. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein remote homology detection and structural alignment using deep learning
indicators: The authors argue that direct DeepBLAST searches are impractical for large databases. Each query requires pairwise alignments whose total runtime grows with database size. (PDF p. 2).
The GPU implementation batches differentiable alignments. The authors report runtime about ten times faster than the naive CPU implementation. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: An Algorithm for the Longest Common Subsequence and Substring Problem for Multiple Strings
indicators: The author attributes correctness to Claims 1–5 and states O(m1 × … × ms × n1 × … × nt) time and space complexity. (PDF p. 17).
The reported outcome is a correctness statement and asymptotic time and space bounds for Algorithm A. (PDF p. 17).

papers.title: The String-to-String Correction Problem
indicators: The time and space complexity are established as proportional to the product of sequence lengths O(mn). (PDF p. 2).
The quadratic time and space complexity O(mn) becomes prohibitive for long sequences without heuristics. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Approximating the Longest Common Subsequence problem within a sub-polynomial factor in linear time
indicators: Lemma 6 converts a Block-LIS approximation with additive error into an LCS approximation factor of (1+o(1))·f(n log n). Its runtime is t(O(n log n),n)+O(n). (PDF p. 4).
Subsampling reduces the direct n^{1+o(1)} runtime to O(n), while retaining a sub-polynomial approximation factor. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: BIMSA: accelerating long sequence alignment using processing-in-memory
indicators: The authors argue that BiWFA remains limited by data movement despite its O(s) memory use and O(ns) runtime. (PDF p. 2).
BIMSA-Hybrid transfers selected alignments to the CPU. This substantially reduces runtime for the tested heterogeneous long-read datasets. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: A Special Case of the Maximal Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The stated running time is O(n log n). A restricted integer case permits O(n log log n) time. (PDF p. 2).
The abstract states an O(n log n) running time for the restricted common subsequence problem. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: BAli-Phy version 3: model-based co-estimation of alignment and phylogeny
indicators: The real-data analysis tests runtime improvements over an earlier version. (PDF p. 3).
The scaling benchmark shows quadratic runtime growth with taxon count for version 2.3.8 and linear growth for version 3.4.1. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast text searching: allowing errors
indicators: For exact matching with a pattern that fits in one word, running time depends mainly on text length rather than text content or alphabet size. (PDF p. 2).
The authors describe the Myers–Miller comparison as unfair because that algorithm supports more general cost functions and has running time independent of the error count. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Accelerating Cryptanalysis with the Method of Four Russians
indicators: Bard describes M4RI for dense Boolean linear systems. The paper gives a cost analysis and experimental runtime measurements. (PDF p. 1).
Runtime measurements are divided by modeled matrix memory-operation counts to estimate a rate of 1.11 × 10^8 operations per second on the author's PC. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: A*PA2: Up to 19× Faster Exact Global Alignment
indicators: The goal is to combine A*PA's near-linear runtime on similar sequences with the efficiency of dynamic programming. (PDF p. 1).

Runtime measurements show that block computation usually dominates. Traceback takes about half the time on 1 kbp sequences. Heuristic initialization takes about one quarter on reads longer than 500 kbp. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: Edit Distance in Near-Linear Time: it’s a Constant Factor
indicators: The authors present a randomized constant-factor approximation for edit distance. For each fixed ε > 0, its running time is O(n^(1+ε)). (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A survey of sequence-to-graph mapping algorithms in the pangenome era
indicators: SOPanG searches elastic-degenerate strings with Shift-Or bit parallelism. The stated time complexity is O(N⌈m/w⌉), with support for k mismatches. (PDF p. 19).
The authors report a several-fold runtime reduction for PaSGAL compared with VG without heuristics. The supplied excerpt gives no benchmark configuration. (PDF p. 16).

papers.title: Analysis of Evolutionary Algorithms for the Longest Common Subsequence Problem
indicators: The study seeks theoretical runtime guarantees for evolutionary algorithms after earlier studies reported good empirical performance on LCS. (PDF p. 2).

The authors use specific difficult instances to assess worst-case performance. They state that the results can also give large average-case lower bounds under a uniform distribution over inputs of equal length. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Maximal common subsequence algorithms
indicators: The maximality checker has linear running time because its search indices move in only one direction. (PDF p. 8).
Theorem 3 states the correctness and O(n) running time of ifMCS for an input that is already a common subsequence. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: MUSCLE: a multiple sequence alignment method with reduced time and space complexity
indicators: The study aims to explain the MUSCLE algorithm and techniques that improve alignment accuracy or computational complexity. (PDF p. 1).
Table 2 gives total space complexity O(N² + L²) and time complexity O(N⁴ + NL²). Progressive alignment alone takes O(N³ + NL²) time. (PDF p. 17).

papers.title: An Improved Longest Common Subsequence Algorithm for Reducing Memory Complexity in Global Alignment of DNA Sequences
indicators: The authors report tests on DNA sequences up to 100 kb. They retain O(MN) time complexity and report lower memory use than full-table LCS. (PDF p. 5).
The authors state that SB_LCS retains O(MN) time complexity. Reconstruction adds some time relative to ordinary LCS. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: On Computing the Length of Longest Increasing Subsequences
indicators: The algorithm takes O(n log n) total time. Its worst-case comparison count is n log n − n log log n + O(n). (PDF p. 3).
Fredman proves a matching worst-case comparison lower bound, up to an additive O(n) term. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Fast, accurate construction of multiple sequence alignments from protein language embeddings
indicators: The authors report higher alignment accuracy on BAliBASE and HOMSTRAD than all tested baselines. Runtime grows approximately linearly over the tested sequence counts. (PDF p. 10).
Runtime scaling has a log-scale slope of 1.01 when the smallest subset is excluded. The 95% confidence interval is 0.798–1.216. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: Improving the Worst Case Performance of the Hunt-Szymanski Strategy for the Longest Common Subsequence of Two Strings
indicators: The proposed longest common subsequence algorithm follows a schedule similar to Hunt–Szymanski while improving worst-case efficiency. (PDF p. 2).
The abstract states an O(mn) worst-case time bound for the proposed algorithm. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Computing a Longest Increasing Subsequence of Length k in Time O(n log log k)
indicators: Express the running time in terms of output length k and improve the previous O(n log log n) bound. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and accurate protein structure search with Foldseek
indicators: The authors report large runtime reductions relative to conventional structural aligners, with some loss of search sensitivity relative to Dali and TM-align. (PDF p. 2).
Runtime tests used a 64-core AMD EPYC 7702P server with 1,024 GB RAM. SCOPe runtimes for TM-align, Dali, and CE were estimated from 10% of queries. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Efficient seeding for error-prone sequences with SubseqHash2
indicators: SIMD reduces the stated runtime to O(Nnk) when d states fit the supported parallel computation. The reported supported range extends to d = 32. (PDF p. 3).
SubseqHash2 and SubseqHash had nearly identical collision probabilities at equal repetition counts. SubseqHash2 was up to 50 times faster on the Oxford Nanopore runtime dataset. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: End-to-end learning of multiple sequence alignments
indicators: The implementation uses JAX compilation and automatic differentiation. Vectorization across sequence length and batch dimensions reduces runtime. (PDF p. 3).

Runtime tests compared forward passes and combined forward–backward passes against a smooth Needleman–Wunsch implementation. They also compared vectorized and naive versions of the authors' code. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast and exact gap-affine partial order alignment
indicators: The authors aim to reduce runtime and memory use while preserving optimal sequence-to-graph alignment. (PDF p. 2).
The authors measured complete MSA runtime and memory for POASTA and SPOA. They also compared abPOA, which uses heuristic banding. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Bit-parallel sequence-to-graph alignment
indicators: For Shift-And, the runtime is O(|V| + ceil(m/w)|E|) on acyclic graphs and O(|V| + m|E|) on cyclic graphs. Here, m is query length and w is machine word size. (PDF p. 2).
For bitvector alignment, the runtime is O(|V| + ceil(m/w)|E| log w) on acyclic graphs and O(|V| + m|E| log w) on cyclic graphs. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: A Faster Algorithm Computing String Edit Distances
indicators: The aim is to improve the asymptotic time of the Wagner–Fischer algorithm, whose time is proportional to the product of the string lengths. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Computing the longest topological common subsequence of a symbol-wise totally ordered directed acyclic graph and a sequence
indicators: The runtime analysis assigns O(|G|²) time to reachability preprocessing and O(|G|²|B|) time to each sequence-position iteration. (PDF p. 7).
The author derives a total running time of O(|G|²|B|²). Here |G| counts vertices and |B| is sequence length. (PDF p. 7).

papers.title: Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (Unless SETH is False)
indicators: The authors seek a conditional explanation for the near-quadratic running time of known exact edit-distance algorithms. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Building pangenome graphs
indicators: The authors report that a tenfold increase in genome count required a 44-fold runtime increase with sparsification, compared with the 100-fold increase expected from quadratic scaling. (PDF p. 2).
For 142 yeast genomes, sparsification reduced runtime from 20.46 to 10.11 hours and memory from 119.68 to 80.25 GB. F-scores were 0.971758 and 0.972030, respectively. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Efficient merged longest common subsequence algorithms for similar sequences
indicators: The algorithms address both unrestricted merging and merging with block constraints. Their runtime depends on the difference between target length and answer length. (PDF p. 1).
The runtime includes the factor r − L + 1. This factor becomes small when the answer covers nearly all of the target. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: An O(ND) Difference Algorithm and Its Variations
indicators: The author presents a linear-space refinement and a suffix-tree variation with O(N log N + D²) worst-case time. (PDF p. 1).
The refinements aim to reduce storage and improve expected or worst-case runtime. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Fast and accurate multiple-protein-sequence alignment at scale with FAMSA2
indicators: The authors report strong accuracy across structural, evolutionary, and functional tests. The medoid tree variant reduces runtime while retaining much of this accuracy. (PDF p. 3).
The authors aim to align millions of protein sequences with high accuracy and practical runtime. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Parasail: SIMD C Library for Global, Semi-Global, and Local Pairwise Sequence Alignments
indicators: The library implements several vectorization methods and selects a supported instruction set at runtime. (PDF p. 3).
The alignment recurrence tracks substitution, deletion, and insertion scores. Its time complexity is O(mn) for sequence lengths m and n. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Accurate multiple alignment of distantly related genome sequences using filtered spaced word matches as anchor points
indicators: Runtime tests use E. coli/Shigella, Roseobacter, and fungal genome datasets. They compare both Mugsy variants and Cactus. (PDF p. 6).
FSWM increases total Mugsy runtime for distant genomes. The authors suggest that its greater sensitivity and larger number of anchors explain this increase. (PDF p. 6).

papers.title: On the Complexity of Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: Table 1 compares asymptotic running times with prior algorithms for edit distance, arbitrary linear costs, and affine gaps. The new bound matches the listed best edit-distance bound and improves the listed bounds for the other two settings. (PDF p. 2).
The affine-gap extension has the same time and space complexity as the linear-gap algorithm. (PDF p. 13).

papers.title: Fast and Accurate Short Read Alignment with Burrows–Wheeler Transform
indicators: The authors report accuracy similar to MAQ with substantially shorter runtime. BWA also produces mapping qualities and SAM output. (PDF p. 1).
Comparisons included MAQ, SOAPv2, and Bowtie. Confident mappings used tool-specific uniqueness rules or mapping quality thresholds. Runtime used one 2.5 GHz Xeon E5420 core. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: MMseqs2 Enables Sensitive Protein Sequence Searching for the Analysis of Massive Data Sets
indicators: Ungapped alignment has linear time complexity along a candidate diagonal. Smith–Waterman alignment has quadratic time complexity. (PDF p. 2).
Runtime tests duplicated queries 100-fold. For SWIPE, BLAST, and RAPsearch2, the authors instead multiplied the original query-set runtime by 100. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Gapped BLAST and PSI-BLAST: A New Generation of Protein Database Search Programs
indicators: Runtime analysis separates overhead, hit qualification, ungapped extension, and gapped extension. (PDF p. 5).
The runtime breakdown assigns 100 relative time units to original BLAST and 33 to gapped BLAST. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: Exact global alignment using A* with chaining seed heuristic and match pruning
indicators: Develop a practical exact aligner with near-linear empirical runtime for long related sequences. (PDF p. 1).
Synthetic experiments use uniform random sequences up to 10 million bases. Runtime scaling is reported at 4% and 12% divergence against EDLIB and BIWFA. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: Faster algorithms for RNA-folding using the Four-Russians method
indicators: Improve serial and parallel runtime for the maximum non-crossing base-pair problem. (PDF p. 1).
Serial runtime measurements average 10 sequences of approximately equal length. Programs are written in C++ and compiled with the highest optimization settings. (PDF p. 10).

papers.title: Recognition and Complexity of Point Visibility Graphs
indicators: The authors investigate the computational complexity of recognizing point visibility graphs in the Euclidean plane. (PDF p. 1).
Recognizing point visibility graphs is ER-complete, establishing that the problem is NP-hard. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: Fast and accurate de novo genome assembly from long uncorrected reads
indicators: The authors report comparable assembly quality and substantial runtime reductions against Canu and FALCON on six long-read data sets. (PDF p. 2).
The authors argue that miniasm's speed is useful only if consensus generation can improve its sequence accuracy without a large runtime cost. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: M2Align: parallel multiple sequence alignment with a multi-objective metaheuristic
indicators: It stores gap information and evaluates candidate alignments in parallel. Tests on BAliBASE show reduced runtime with up to 20 cores. (PDF p. 2).
Serial profiling of BAliBASE instance BB20001 identifies solution evaluation as the main runtime cost. This motivates parallel evaluation. (PDF p. 5).

papers.title: HHblits: Lightning-Fast Iterative Protein Sequence Searching by HMM–HMM Alignment
indicators: Runtime tests used 100 random queries on one Xeon 2.9 GHz core. HHblits searched UniProt20; PSI-BLAST and HMMER3 searched UniProt. (PDF p. 2).
Median single-iteration runtime was 31 seconds for HHblits, 67 seconds for PSI-BLAST, and 177 seconds for HMMER3. Mean runtimes were 73, 86, and 308 seconds. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Ultrafast and Memory-Efficient Alignment of Short DNA Sequences to the Human Genome
indicators: Map massive volumes of next-generation sequencing short reads to mammalian genomes with minimal memory and runtime. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: String editing under pattern constraints
indicators: Computational complexity is analyzed using parameterized complexity theory and reductions to hitting set. (PDF p. 14).
Computational complexity becomes intractable for general context-free language constraints without parameter bounds. (PDF p. 15).

papers.title: GraphAligner: Rapid and Versatile Sequence-to-Graph Alignment
indicators: The authors report a 13-fold runtime improvement over vg on variation graphs. Their human-read correction pipeline more than halves the error rate relative to FMLRC. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Protein remote homology detection and structural alignment using deep learning
indicators: TM-Vec converts ProtT5 residue embeddings into 512-dimensional protein vectors with a twin neural network. Transformer layers, average pooling, dropout and fully connected layers produce the vectors. Training minimizes L1 error between cosine similarity and reference TM-scores. (PDF p. 12).

papers.title: Clifford Group Equivariant Neural Network Layers for Protein Structure Prediction
indicators: The authors replace linear layers in a protein-coordinate projector with Clifford Group Equivariant Neural Network layers. (PDF p. 3).
A Graph Transformer encodes biochemical node and edge features. A separate 3D projector converts its node representations into alpha-carbon coordinates. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: A trimodal protein language model enables advanced protein searches
indicators: ProTrek learns a shared representation of protein sequence, structure, and function text through bidirectional contrastive learning. (PDF p. 1).
The model uses an ESM sequence encoder and a BERT text encoder. Genuine modality pairs are brought closer in embedding space, while negative pairs are separated. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: pLM-BLAST: distant homology detection based on direct
indicators: Global mode uses Needleman-Wunsch with the embedding-based substitution matrix and a zero gap penalty. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Fast, sensitive detection of protein homologs using deep dense retrieval
indicators: DHR retrieves protein homologs through learned sequence embeddings and dot-product similarity. (PDF p. 2).
The authors argue that learned embeddings can retain structural and evolutionary information that sequence similarity searches miss. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Accurate Prediction of Protein Structures and Interactions Using a Three-Track Neural Network
indicators: RoseTTAFold exchanges information between sequence alignments, residue-pair geometry, and three-dimensional coordinates in a three-track neural network. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: BetaAlign: a deep learning approach for multiple sequence alignment
indicators: They assess training size, training duration, transfer learning, transformer architecture, and training within restricted indel-parameter ranges. (PDF p. 2).
Transfer-learning tests compare initial training, repeated training on the same dataset, and training on more complex datasets before returning to the original dataset. (PDF p. 10).

papers.title: Bilingual language model for protein sequence and structure
indicators: The authors aim to model protein sequence and structure in one language model. (PDF p. 1).
The authors propose future uses in structural phylogenetics, embedding-based alignment, and MSA generation. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: Deep embedding and alignment of protein sequences
indicators: The encoder has six transformer layers, 12 attention heads per layer, and 768-dimensional embeddings. Bilinear functions produce substitution scores. Softplus transforms produce nonnegative gap penalties. (PDF p. 9).

Training combines masked language modeling on UniRef50, alignment learning from Pfam-A seed, and homology classification. Random flanks extend Pfam domains to create local alignment examples. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Rewriting protein alphabets with language models
indicators: A neural network quantizes protein language model embeddings into 20 discrete letters. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: End-to-end learning of multiple sequence alignments
indicators: The Learned Alignment Module constructs differentiable multiple sequence alignments with smooth Smith–Waterman. A downstream learning objective can update the alignment. (PDF p. 2).
Learned similarity scores depend on residue context and vary across protein families. They are not fixed functions of residue identities. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning (Alphafold)
indicators: Predict accurate protein structures by learning residue distances and minimizing the resulting potential. (PDF p. 2).
They argue that a differentiable learned potential permits structure generation with limited sampling. (PDF p. 2).

papers.title: Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold
indicators: AlphaFold predicts protein atomic coordinates with a neural network that uses sequence, MSA, and structural information. (PDF p. 3).
Initial training uses 256-residue crops and batches of 128 on 128 TPU v3 cores. Fine-tuning uses 384-residue crops, larger MSAs, and a lower learning rate. (PDF p. 8).

papers.title: Robust Deep Learning–Based Protein Sequence Design Using ProteinMPNN
indicators: The authors introduce ProteinMPNN, a deep learning model for de novo protein sequence design on target backbones. (PDF p. 1).
An autoregressive message-passing graph neural network maps backbone geometry to amino acid probabilities. (PDF p. 3).

papers.title: Protein Secondary Structure Prediction Based on Position-Specific Scoring Matrices
indicators: Online back-propagation uses momentum 0.9 and learning rate 0.005. Training stops when performance declines on the 10% of training data reserved for monitoring. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Improving spliced alignment by modeling splice sites with deep learning
indicators: Minisplice uses a small one-dimensional convolutional neural network to score candidate splice sites. (PDF p. 1).

papers.title: PLMSearch: Protein language model powers accurate and fast sequence search for remote homology
indicators: PLMSearch uses protein language model embeddings and Pfam clans to search for homologous proteins from sequence input. (PDF p. 6).

SS-predictor training uses PyTorch 1.7.1, ADAM, mean squared error, batch size 100, learning rate 1e-6, and 200 epochs. TM-align supplies training targets from SCOPe40-train and CATHS40. ESM-1b parameters remain fixed. (PDF p. 9).

papers.title: Accurate Structure Prediction of Biomolecular Interactions with AlphaFold 3
indicators: The authors aim to predict complexes with many molecular types in one deep-learning framework. (PDF p. 1).
Training adjusts dataset sampling probabilities and uses a weighted metric for early stopping. These measures address uneven learning and possible overfitting. (PDF p. 4).

papers.title: Diagnosing protein sequence search in the era of language
indicators: Across eight methods, the authors report greater diagnostic stability for alignment-based search than for fully embedding-based search. (PDF p. 6).
The model-manipulation test applies only to methods with learned PLM representations. (PDF p. 11).

papers.title: Protein embedding based alignment
indicators: The authors sought an embedding-based local aligner that could support remote homology searches. (PDF p. 3).
The authors propose using PEbA to align candidate hits from embedding-based search tools such as knnProtT5. (PDF p. 15).
